paragraphs.text: PREFACE TO THE PASCHAL WORK OF SEDULIUS

Guest, whoever you are who share in the Paschal feast and do not disdain to recline on our couches: if you come as a dear friend, lay aside the lofty arch of your raised brow. Do not look here for the work of a skilled book. Instead, gladly receive the modest fare of a small table, take it contentedly, and be glad to be filled in mind rather than with food. Or if you are drawn instead to a great abundance of rich things, and as a person of refined taste you expect choice luxuries, you should take your fill at the banquets of noble and learned men, whose many courses cannot be listed. There you will certainly find whatever the waves of the sea nourish for eating, whatever the fertile earth supplies, and whatever holds its body aloft among the clouds on balanced wings. On the very platters, too, which are jewelled with exceedingly costly variety, honey glows golden in its nectarous combs, and the honeycomb set in golden baskets matches the metal with its colour. But we have plucked a cheap vegetable grown from the seeds of a poor man's garden, and we are seen to serve it on a dish of red earthenware, with goodwill rather than splendour.
BOOK ONE

The pagan poets make a habit of commending the trifles of their fabulous songs with the pomp of noble words. Whether with the clamour of buskined tragedy, or the comic foulness of the laughable Geta, or the measures of any metrical art you please, they hand down the wicked deeds of ancient times, and with a reed pen tracing on papyrus from the Nile's flood they even pass on things composed with the art of shameful storytelling. Why then should I keep the wonderful and saving mighty works of Christ to myself in silence? On the ten-stringed psaltery I practise the songs of David's melody among the choirs of blessed teaching and reverently answer the spiritual words. Surely I ought to take up the work of truth, and with the instrument of faithful speech I ought not to be silent about the gifts of heavenly grace. For the service of the human heart and mind is owed more justly to no one than to the almighty Lord, who established the senses and founded hearts, so that the material ever devoted to its Creator should not abandon its own maker. It is not fitting that what he has made, which is his by right, should be withdrawn from him or perish. In everlasting dominion in the heavenly heights he has one power with the Father: equal brightness of splendour, the undivided loftiness of a shared summit, equal honour, the same might, a shared eminence, a kingdom without end in time, a beginning ever abiding in unbroken eternity, glory that shares in the fellowship of the sceptre, and a like majesty. This is the road that leads to the dwelling of salvation; this is the path that lies open to firm steps toward the Paschal gifts. Here we shall lay the foundations of our work. Here, then, turn your sick minds, all of you, and apply this medicine to your deadly diseases, you on whom the empty aim of harmful disputation creeps, and whom the incurable discipline of Attic teaching wounds with the poison of Cecropian doctrine. Then, when you breathe in the life-giving airs, the breath of the divine law and the fragrance of the sweetness of glowing grace, you may leave behind from now on, with a purer mind, the gluttony of Athenian filth. Why, sons of Theseus, do you wander in dark errors around the windings of the labyrinth, and, with tangled footsteps and the way out lost, roam blindly through the gloomy caves in their mazes? Why do you still prefer the wild vine to the good vine? Why do you rank the little willow above the shining rose gardens? What good will it do to trust with empty worship in images of stone and figures of bronze, or to condemn souls to slavery to profane shrines and metal objects of veneration? Spare yourselves, I beg you, spare yourselves now the squalid clods of sandy dust and the bare dryness of barren fields, where the land has never known how to repay the sweating farmer's labour with a fertile reward from a pregnant womb. Do not pluck from the shoots of bloody turf poisonous nourishment of deadly juice, which, ever friendly to the foods of hell, cannot serve life, only death. Rather, enter by the clear streams of a pure spring into the pleasant meadows of flowering grass and the lovely approaches of the blessed abode. There the fertility of life-giving seeds, quickened by divine waters, nourishes a crop that grows once the roughness of thorns has been uprooted. Through the vast abundance of its manifold fruit it can already be God's harvest, and, opening the hope of future reward, it may store its fruit in hundredfold heaps in the greatest of barns.

Almighty God of undivided and eternal godhead! You hold the whole world by your holy nod. You made firm the structure of heaven by the work of your fingers and founded its fabric by your mighty word. You set bounds that forbid the rushing madness of the surging sea to overwhelm the edge of the neighbouring land. You make the face of the radiant sun and the horned face of the moon border on day and night, and you dispense the alternations of both lights with the holy balance of your governance. You alone gather and you alone know the number of the stars, their powers, signs, names, places, courses and times. You gave life to the torpid limbs of the raw earth, filling it with living bodies in their varied motions. You condemned to death the man who ate the fruit of the tree in forbidden presumption, but afterwards you raise him up by the sacrament of a better food, and by the drinking of spotless blood you preserve him from the voluptuous deceit of the viper's bite. When the race of mankind had been utterly drowned and buried by the sudden flood of the rising deluge, except for those whom the ark had guarded, you restored it and multiplied it again from a single stock. You did this to reveal, by a demonstration of mystical power, that what the sins of the flesh had killed was to be washed in the one baptism of the whole world, fenced about by the faithful protection of wood. Graciously show me that way; show your suppliant now that path which directs the footsteps of the few along a narrow track to the walls of the city of salvation, namely Jerusalem, the Lord's city, which bears our Passover through the passion of Christ. Then through this city, which offers the hospitality of bodily grace, we may be worthy to reach that homeland of spiritual glory. And let your word, Lord, be a lamp to my feet, so that the brightness of the right road may lead me to those places of flowering grass where the good shepherd keeps a shining fold, and where the whole white-robed flock follows the Lamb of the virgin ewe, most pure in snowy brightness. The way is not hard if you deign to offer yourself as guide. All things lie under your power; all nature yields to your commands and passes into opposite forms and shapes at your sovereign bidding. If you wish the yearly crops to turn golden in icy seasons, sluggish winter brings forth a reaper quick with his sickle. If you bid the vine bring forth heavy tendrils in the mild weather of springtime, when the earth shines covered with its first mantle of flowers, the vintner, dancing in a stream of new wine, will press out the nectarous insides of the happy grape with the welcome injury of his drunken heel. And all the turning seasons, with their fruits changed, will not refuse to serve their Creator. Indeed, hoary faith gives proof of divine wonders, and the ancient origins of the fathers of old bear witness. The immortal signs of heavenly power endure and are not abolished, though the ages pass and time grows old. Of these, with the fear of a trembling wit, I scarcely allow my mind and weak heart to touch on at least a few in bold narration, as someone entering a very dense forest might strive to touch a few branches with the very tips of his fingers. For even if a human body were supplied with a hundred mouths at once, and an iron voice never ceased to cry out with the movements of a hundred tongues, who could set forth all these things? Neither the thick-set stars of heaven nor the thirsty sand of the sea could match their number.

First of all, ever since the confused matter of things called chaos rose into the bright face of the world through the fashioning Word, Enoch, most pleasing and beloved to God, attained a living glory. Passing beyond the measure of human nature through countless courses of years, he paid his due to the earth by being born, but he made a marvel of death, from which he was taken away.

Sarah's limbs were already withering, faint with old age. Her blood, spent by the decay of great age, had condemned the veins of her aged body to barrenness, with no hope left of offspring. Then, made fertile by union with her elderly husband, she suddenly felt her cold womb swell. Her heart swelled with a new birth, and the trembling mother held the son born of her late happiness to her breasts for milk, in hope of a future nation and people.

His father offered him as a gift to God, though the promise of him had come when all hope was gone. The boy stood with his throat bared, and a ram became the burnt offering. O spotless mind of the holy priest! He rejected human things and looked to the divine; in denying his son life, he gained it for him. Abraham drew the sword to strike, and the Lord exchanged the sacrifice in order to spare. Clearly a great mystery was enacted in this devotion: that Christ, the gentle lamb, would offer himself willingly as a victim for the life of mankind.

Lot was fleeing Sodom as it was about to perish. His wife, with the boldness of careless presumption, looked back at what she had escaped and was changed, remaining as a statue of salt, not for wisdom but for punishment. For no one who has once scorned the dangers of the world and then turns back to them again with headlong desire will enjoy the gladness of pleasant salvation. Nor is that ploughman worthy to rejoice in the coming fertility of his crops who turns his face backward, confuses the furrow of the ploughshare that ought to be held firm in a straight course, and scatters the order of his past labour.

A bush, once wrapped in harmless fires, was seen burning without burning. Its material gave no fuel to the flames, nor, though seized by the fire of the surrounding heat, did it suffer the damage of burnt wood. So tempered was the touch of the divine kindling that the flame caressed the glowing branches, and in the leaves was seen splendour, not punishment.

The tractable nature of a gentle rod was changed into an ungentle and intractable serpent. Twisting in sinuous coils, it moved like a viper and darted its three-forked tongue. It swallowed the pair of snakes produced by hostile trickery, and then by a stiffening change it took on again the proper form of a staff.

The waters were rolled back on either side and held up in the sea by divine construction, and a crowd crossed on foot through the depths that lay hidden beneath the waves. The sea stood on every side like a wall, and the land, stripped of the covering of its kindred flood, remained bare, while the people walked through the sea, with the sea absent from their steps, and took a road of watery dryness that was hospitable to strangers. Nature, ordered to relax its constancy for a little while, changed its path. The countless multitude that crossed the plains of slippery salt saw, without knowing it, the rudimentary mystery of baptism, having passed through the saving straits of the waters with Christ as their guide. Thus indeed the prophet sang, signifying these things: "The voice of the Lord is upon many waters." Who, then, doubts that the "voice" means the Word? And who would deny that the Word of the Father is Christ? As founder of the Old and the New Testament, he opened by his coming the immense abyss of the first law. By his newer teaching, as though the masses of the waves had been removed, the age that followed could advance safely along the path of open liberty, fearing no danger from the inmost depths.

Why should I tell how the countless throngs of that same people, in the desert expanses of the land, condemned to the barrenness of every kind of sustenance, received the food of angels and the bread of heavenly grace? There a nectarous cloud from the heavenly majesty, sprinkling the people with dew, poured out feasts from the rains and plentiful food from the showers.

Again, the army burned with thirst amid fields parched by violent heat, where the land lay languishing in its usual burning and springs were denied, and where the failing nature of water had taken away all hope of drinking and of living alike. Then the torpor shut up within the astonished rock suddenly overflowed from the surging cliff into a foaming stream, and the veins of the dry, fasting marble poured out abundant drink for all. In these three things, then, already announcing the great sacraments of his mystery, Christ was in the sea, Christ in the bread, Christ in the rock.
A she-ass, a cheap and stupid beast, terrified by the sight of an angelic power, addresses her rider in words, and the uncouth cry of a braying tongue unfolds into the speech of a human voice.

The sun, at the very summit of the sky, reined in the swift course of its panting flame and stood fixed over Gibeon. Evening was postponed, and the sun held its light in an unusual delay of the day. Nor did the moon, moved by its own laws, pass beyond the threshold of its sluggish station or keep the order of its accustomed step, until the sword of the victorious army, joined in alliance with heavenly aid, utterly cut down the enemy's strength. Indeed, the very stars, now serving, saw through the mystery of a like name that the Lord Jesus would come, his name going before him.

Contrary to the order of nature, ravens sustained Elijah with daily meals. The bird given over to the greed of its voracious beak, which readily feeds easy prey to its hollow throat, brought him food untouched, with fasting bites. Now good and faithful to Elijah, it washed away the guilt it had incurred during the flood of waters, when it was once wicked and faithless to Noah on the earth. But Elijah, being full of God, showed many miracles on earth and, through the spirit, as if by a bountiful inheritance, passed on the gift of his own power to a friend worthy to succeed him. Then he was caught up by fiery horses and chariots through those heights of clear serenity, where the lighter way of the pure track keeps no ruts of a glowing wheel on the heavenly plain, since no rim sinks into it. So he sought the regions on the right hand, of a greater expanse, so that, shining in the chariot of heavenly triumph and relying on a long life, he scorned the goal at the end of the human course. How well, how fittingly and deservedly, the majesty of the shining path smiled on Elijah's brightness, even in his name! For if in the Greek language a single letter could be changed by its accent, the name would seem to express specifically "sun."

Hezekiah, a most righteous king, had reached the very end of his life. In his mercy, or by right, the Lord added fifteen years to him for his safety. He closed the threshold of death, which had already opened, and called his life, languishing at its setting, back to its origin at the rising.

Jonah was thrown into the waves of the sea by the panic of the anxious ship and hidden in the belly of the swallowing whale. Though set in the sea, he did not feel the waters, for he had entered a life-giving tomb so that he would not die. Safe in the gentlest of custody beneath a devouring belly, he was seen to be God's deposit, not prey. Preserved more healthfully by the protection of an enemy, he came to land by being vomited up, not by ship. In this event, by a contrary reversal, the sailor showed savagery and the beast provided a vessel.

With God inspiring them from heaven, the three young men were of one mind in heart: they despised and refused the sacred rites of Babylon alike, and accepted the harsh end of death under the cruelty of a tyrant's law. The tyrant's rage, kindled by the fire of Achaemenian fury, surpassed the scorching heat of his own furnace. The youths were bound and thrust into the midst of the pyres, but the pyre did not dare to touch them. Burning only in heart, they overcame the punishment imposed for the image, as the penalty failed. O how great are the salvation and glory of believers! The force of the furnace was quenched and grew numb before the flames of a hotter faith.

The author of so wicked a judgment did not escape a punishment worthy of his deed. Because, seized by senseless madness, he had despised the laws of human kindness, he lived like a beast in the forests. He followed the companionship of cattle and exchanged the dainty pleasures of the court banquet for rustic fare, feeding on hay and drinking from the river. Seven times passed while he was seen in this hideous form, shaggy and wandering through forests and mountains.

No less afterwards, in the reign of Darius, while fury imitated the madness of the past, Daniel, the greatest glory of the Hebrews, was shut up with beasts goaded by hunger, and the innocent body of a simple soul was assigned to be devoured by savage bites. Yet the beasts became gentle and calm. Rather than tear the holy limbs with frenzied teeth in their hunger, they now began to love their hunger. Their rage softened and lowered its terrible looks, and anger rested more gently in their savage jaws; so it taught the lions, forgetful of their native ferocity, to keep their prey unharmed.

Tell me, stubborn nature, where are your laws after such things, since he has so often taken your rights away from you? Who commanded the underworld not to know the man who was taken up? Who gave a fertile old age to a barren wife, made a beast come willingly to the altar, turned a woman's form into a statue of salt, showed branches blazing with fire yet not burning, turned a staff into a snake, opened a way on foot through the waves of the sea, poured nectarous manna from raining clouds, and drove out waters from the parched depths of a rock? Who let the mouth of a dumb beast speak human words, held the elements in a long halt with their courses fixed, fed a man by the service of birds and carried him to heaven in a chariot drawn by flashing horses, granted three five-year spans of life to a dying king, and made the belly of a wild predator a harbour for a shipwrecked man? Who bathed the young men's limbs with starry dew in the furnace, made a wandering king a fellow diner with wild beasts and cattle in thorny pastures, and taught lions to spare their prey and not to love plunder? Surely your laws are subject to the Creator of all things, by the workings of whose word all things, whether known or hidden, stand fashioned and lie beneath him as the foundations of his work. Creation follows the command of the one who orders it, wherever the divine decree draws it with a nod.

Alas for the wretched people who, bent on vain worship, devote the foolish service of a perverse heart to images they themselves have carved, and who abandon their own maker to venerate the likenesses made by their own hands! What madness is this? What great insanity mocks their minds, so that a man whole in his limbs worships a foul bird, a most obscene cow, a twisted serpent and a half-human dog?

Some, blinded in their clouded minds, hold the opinion that the sun should be reckoned the begetter of things, because it floods the tracts and spaces of the earth with the light of clear serenity and never ceases to traverse the regions of the sky and the stars with flaming speed. Yet from this very unstable motion, which the wandering fire performs in its rapid courses, it is clear that it is a servant, not a god. Keeping the order of a fixed arrangement, it now rises, and now, inclining toward its setting as the hours decline, shares its turns with the night. Nor is it always present everywhere. And it saw none of the first beginnings of the world, for two days had already passed without a sun before the provident Begetter appointed it to shine from the beginning of the third day.
So too many pay superfluous vows to the moon, though they see it always waxing and waning at the appointed times of the months.
So too they never cease to sacrifice to the stars, which are put to flight by the face of the morning light when the night departs and is driven away.

This man worships the waters, that one the flames. But they do not dare to set side by side things that are opposite by nature, lest in closer discord either the hotter fire dry up the weaker waters, or the pyre, no match for mighty waves, suddenly die out, extinguished.

Another sets up altars at the roots of trees and lays out feasts there, and never ceases to pray tearfully to branches and trunks to guard his children, house, farms, marriage, servants and wealth. Man of wood, why do you entreat wood? You waste your effort shouting to the deaf; you wait for answers from the mute and will hear nothing. Wood keeps houses standing only in this way: when it is cut down with axes and props up the overhanging roofs, or when it is laid on the hearth, set alight, and serves to cook food.

Some, more insanely still, are worshippers of vegetables. Watering deities in their gardens, they prove themselves the true worshippers of dried-up transplanted gods. But it is shameful now to relate more of such things, lest on the page of holy religion, while we chastise the many errors of folly, either the rough bramble scorch the lilies, so soft in their great beauty, or the thistle and the thorn-bush armed with spiny prickles spring up among the purple violet-beds of the flowering field. So it is enough by way of rebuke that we have mocked the monsters worshipped through human error, or rather wept for such acts with pity. Now it is good to keep to the course of the path we began, to climb the lofty mountain with a firm step, and to strive with all our strength to reach the city, the source of our liberty. It is the house of tranquil peace, the safe dwelling of salvation, the everlasting lodging of liberty. For if the poet of secular letters sang thus of an earthly city of a mortal kingdom, founded by a mortal builder: "And what was so great a cause for you to see Rome? Liberty...," how much more should we believe that the rights of everlasting liberty belong to the city of the heavenly kingdom, which the Lord God founded as its builder! Of it the prophet of such songs says: "The Lord builds up Jerusalem." And in the following psalm he likewise explained: "Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem; praise your God, O Zion, for he has strengthened the bars of your gates; he has blessed your children within you; he has made peace your borders," and so on. Let us also hear the Creator of all things himself in his Gospels, declaring in sacred speech whose city this is: "I say to you," he says, "do not swear at all, neither by heaven, for it is God's throne, nor by the earth, for it is the footstool of his feet, nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King." It is as if he were saying "mine," which he refrained from stating more openly, so that through the humility of his speech he might reveal the height of his majesty. For so, when he was teaching, he admonished them, saying: "Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart." Here is where the royal hall shines with golden domes, where whoever asks receives, whoever seeks finds, and whoever knocks soon has the door opened to him.
Here is that precious stone which the builders rejected and which shines, set as the head of the corner. Its burden is felt to be very light, and its yoke is proved to be most sweet.

We have therefore recounted, in an orderly arrangement, certain miracles of the Old Testament: those which the Father performed with the Son as his partner and the Holy Spirit present with him. In the same orderly way we shall recount certain miracles of the New Testament: those which the Son performed with the Father as his partner and the Holy Spirit present with him. So the one power of the Godhead, always seen in an inseparable might and a single majesty, is threefold, and in its threefold person it is single. This is the true faith and the firm belief.

This salvation the wretched Arius scorned to keep. While he strove to turn aside from the straight road through the winding bends of a crooked path, he slid into a foul pit and followed the darkness of gloomy Tartarus. He was as empty and void of sense as, at the time of his just punishment, he was emptied in his belly too, when he breathed his last with his bowels poured out. Madman, who thought that the rights of the Father's divinity, which no example of likeness can equal, could be compared to perishable ranks! Among human beings, who are born by the law of the flesh, the son is less than the father, since the father who now comes before the son was himself a son a little before, and there is no doubt that he who is now seen to be a son can become a father. Thus a new offspring runs on through the whole line of descendants, and the forefathers of grandfathers are counted up in vast old age. But the Lord Christ, who is the Word, the power, the wisdom, and all that the Father has, is light risen from light, the only one born of the only one. He is in no way less than the Father, nor is there anything in which he could grow, for he is higher than all things. Indeed, since he was begotten, not created, he bears the name Beginning because of his supremacy. For so, according to John, when the Jews questioned him, he said that he was the beginning. What, then, is the beginning but the lofty summit above which nothing at all is found? He abides ever in the Father, because the Father ever abides in him, and the one head of all things is God of undivided majesty. This is not because the Son is believed to be who the Father is, but because the Son is believed to be what the Father is, as he himself said in the teaching of the Gospel: “I am in the Father and the Father in me.” Then he went on to add: “I and the Father are one.” Let Arius hear that “one” is said; let Sabellius learn that “are” is said. The one flees from the Trinity, the other dissents from the unity: both are equal in error, though they follow different paths. In the same way the authors of pagan doctrines try to contradict one another in their sayings. They thrust out their arms bare from naked shoulders and are ready to hand on nothing by teaching, but only to contend in long disputation. Their wisdom lies there foolish, because the frail learning of worldly wisdom is vain before God. One talks more, another keeps more silent; one disputes while walking, another pronounces while standing; one is always weeping, another never stops laughing. So by different ways an equal madness is seen in them all.

Meanwhile, as we lighten the burden of the journey's toil with talk, and hope and faith together accompany my steps up the steep way, we have laid our difficulty aside and come more pleasantly to the summit of the highest citadel. See, the sacred banners of the cross are already shining; see, the most holy camp of the great king displays a flashing light, and the trumpet of the Lord's post calls out with a heavenly blast. The approach to his gate lies open to his soldiers: let whoever serves in his army enter without fear. The gate of eternity invites you, and that gate is Christ, that is, the Father's voice. You will rejoice in the golden reward of everlasting life, you who manfully handle the heavenly arms of the Lord and show the ornament fixed on your forehead, the sacrament of the faithful sign. Behold, good king, I, the least part of your army, carry the consecrated ornament and the heavenly arms. Grant that I may receive a dwelling of my own here, and count me worthy of a small habitation within the walls of this city, so that, always your inhabitant and your household servant, settled in a little corner of the holy dwelling, I may deserve to be enrolled, the last of all, as a citizen among the citizens of the blessed order on the register of the page of life. I ask for great things indeed, but your greatness is able to give great things, and he offends you more who conceives a doubtful hope of such great goodness.

Christ, assent to my prayers, smile on my prayers, you who, hastening to bring the dying world to life, came down from heaven to the things of earth and deigned to take on human form, taking up what was not your own but not leaving behind what was. Undertaking this, Matthew first set forth the man in general terms; Mark, like a wondrous lion, roared out his cry through the deserts; Luke, beginning with the priestly worship, took the likeness of the young bull; John, with the swoop of a flying eagle, pierced heaven with the majesty of the Word. These four leaders and heralds, singing of you with one voice, range like as many seasons across the wide expanse of the whole world. So too the twelvefold summit of apostolic height and honour, ever shining, imitates in its number the hours and the months, so that, with all things gathered together, the whole year may serve as your soldier. From here, then, recalling the ancient beginnings of the old death, I gladly hasten to the new life, so that we who sowed weeping in Adam may reap joy in Christ, and may be worthy to sing David's song: “Those who sow in tears will reap in joy. Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds; but coming, they will come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves.”
BOOK TWO.

That most wicked serpent had driven the first-created man from the flowery seat of paradise by deceitful arts, and through the allurements of a pleasant taste had made him taste a hidden death that was soon bitter. Nor did the violator of the command alone receive the sentence of divine anger in the loss of life; the human race descending from him also fell under the condition of a long death. Alas, cruel and harmful wife! Or was it rather that treacherous, murderous dragon? He was the treacherous, murderous dragon, but you too were a cruel and harmful wife. Oh, the pain of it! There had been only two, and they were immortal. After the stock began to grow, it perished, and bringing forth ruin it suffered loss from its very seed. What good was it in that age to have many and manifold days? What good was it, in happy spans of life, to pass nine hundred years and, as the tenth generation of descendants grew old, to see their own family's blood already grown foreign to them? For the lot of the human condition, seized in its final course by the last irreparable hour, could in no way escape death, however late it came; and life, brief even across a long age of time, lamented that nothing is lasting that is shut in by an end.

No hope would have promised that a remedy for this evil would ever come. The deadly guilt of the first man made from earth would have swallowed up, in its greedy jaws, all the nations everywhere, even those of the last generation, had not that loving Creator and Founder of all things, whose nature it is to pour out pardon on sins rather than to threaten punishment, deigned to raise up again more firmly, through the same stone, the structure of his work, which had been weak from its very foundation. He did this so that the image made in the likeness of God, which had been living, should not be counted unlike him through death. He bestowed the gift of forgiving mercy, and kept the children's teeth from being set on edge by the fruit that their parents had devoured unripe. Most gentle and now appeased, he granted that boundless love should nourish life again from the very source from which sins had contracted death. And just as a sweet and most delicate rose springs from a thorny bush without harming the mother plant, which it outshines by the grace of its loveliness, so from the stock of guilty Eve came Mary with sacred light, a virgin following after, to wash away the stain of the first virgin. Because our former nature, defiled by vices, had been made subject to the condition of harsh death, so, with Christ being born through a human being, humanity too might be reborn through Christ, and lay aside the foulness of the original stain by the renewal of the old body.

The night [?] of prophecy had often foretold these things, and the archangel Gabriel had announced them to Mary in person. Soon afterwards the conception of the faithful Word, breathed in by the Spirit, remained in the womb of the believing girl, and the heavenly offspring, who by his nod allowed all things to be born, lay hidden under the law of birth. The virgin's womb swelled, and her untouched body marveled at the fruitfulness of its inner parts. The mystery of a woman giving birth without a man promised great help to the world, when she, darkened by the blemish of no stain, nourished the life within her swelling womb, soon to be the mother of her own Maker.

Meanwhile the ninth month had passed, and the immortal light of the tenth was shining, and the promise of spiritual grace was made plain in the virgin's child: "And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us," that is, he dwelt in the man whose flesh he deigned to put on. For the infant, small and yet supreme, tiny in his limbs but most exalted in his deity, passing out through the pure chastity of the temple that had received him, did no harm to the body in leaving it, just as he had done it no harm when he came. Truly this is the secret of divine generation: he who entered as guardian of his mother's modesty, and was both conceived and formed while her womb remained closed, is shown to be the witness of the virgin birth. What brightness of new light then filled the borders of the whole world! What joy there was in heaven! What radiance shone forth when Christ, in starry splendor, "like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber," came forth from Mary's womb! His divine beauty seemed to shine with such grace that David's psalm proclaims of him: "You are fairer in form than the children of men; grace is poured out upon your lips," and so on. And rightly it calls him fairer in form than the children of men, for although he took on the appearance of a human incarnation, and in the preaching of the Gospel often called himself the Son of Man, original sin had defiled us, but he did not have it, he who cleansed us by the purity of his birth. O merciful love, so ready to save! So that the yoke of long slavery should not weigh upon us because of the condition of sin, the Lord took on the limbs of a slave. Let us hear the voice of the Apostle Paul, who says: "He emptied himself, taking the form of a slave," and so on. He who has clothed all things born since the beginning of the world allowed his own limbs to be wrapped in swaddling clothes; and he for whom the bounds of heaven are small, for whom the earth is too little and the waves of the sea are not enough, remained whole in a child's body, God lying in a little manger.

Hail, best of mothers, consecrated by giving birth to so great a King, who reigns so unceasingly over things above and things below that his rule, his power and his name know neither beginning nor end. By the shining honor of your blessed womb you are proved to be both mother and virgin at once. No woman at all is found equal to you, none who has gone before you or will come after you in a like glory. You alone, uniquely pleasing to Christ, are compared with no example.

Then, through the joyful message of the angel, shepherds keeping watch over their flock by night were the first to learn that the Lord was born, so that the Shepherd of the world might be made known to shepherds, and the Lamb might be seen to have been born among the flocks. So the Gospel bears witness, saying: "And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army, praising God and saying: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will." The faithful testimony of the Evangelist shows whose kingdom was at stake here, when the multitude of the heavenly army praises God in Christ. Thus, although his creation was human because of his mother's condition, the single fellowship of the Godhead shows that the Father is known in the Son. So they said: "Glory to God in the highest." Certainly the glory of God remained in the highest, for Christ did not leave there when he came. "And on earth peace to men of good will." We must believe that human beings are here called "earth," since we were formed from it by the Lord's hand, who said in rebuking Adam: "For you are earth, and to earth you shall go." For our earth deserved peace after that deadly war in which it fell, when Christ took on the earth of our flesh. For if we suppose that "earth" in this passage means fields and mountains, what peace or what battles can a dumb and inert mass have? That peace, then, came down specially upon those people whom it found capable of good will, so that wherever he who searches hearts and minds sees a sincere intention, there he delights to set up the dwelling of his abode. For this too is peace, and the reasoning of the better will: not to side with the flesh in its struggle against the spirit, but to keep both substances continually in harmonious purity under the rule of the spirit. Nor should we distrust the weakness of the flesh so much that we seem to despair of heavenly help. For the almighty Lord Jesus Christ, who is shown to be the mediator between God and man, took away from us the excuse of bodily frailty: he asks only for the effort of our will, and has reserved the perfecting of good works to his own majesty. The Apostle's teaching explains this, saying: "To will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find"; for to will the good is ours, but to accomplish it belongs to God, who pours his peace upon people of good will. Then the divine word continues, saying:

"Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judah in the days of King Herod, behold, wise men came from the east to Jerusalem, saying: Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? For we have seen his star in the east and have come to worship him. When King Herod heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. And gathering all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where the Christ was to be born. They said to him: In Bethlehem of Judah; for so it is written by the prophet: And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come a leader who will rule my people Israel. Then Herod secretly called the wise men and learned from them the time of the star that had appeared to them. And sending them to Bethlehem, he said: Go and search diligently for the child, and when you have found him, report to me, so that I too may come and worship him." In fitting agreement with the decree of the Scriptures, Christ's birth shone from the east, for it fulfils what the prayer of Zechariah describes: "The East from on high has visited us." David's psalm, too, contains something similar: "In the sun he has set his tabernacle," and so on. By the sun he means the east, the region from which day always rises. Why then, Herod, do you rage so cunningly? Why do you rave so madly? You profess Christ with your tongue but persecute him in your heart, and you hide a mind that is foul and condemned to the darkness of a murky gloom behind the calm of a cheerful face. For you order Christ to be sought, not to be worshipped with the devotion you pretend, but to be killed by the deceit you are plotting. You are badly mistaken and deceived in thinking that he will succeed you, he who reigns first on the royal throne, who neither succeeds anyone nor passes away, but eternally holds the seat of his majesty; you read the law and disregard it, you who threaten the King of kings over your kingdom. This guilt is beyond words; this treachery is without excuse: for you are trying to destroy the one you had promised to worship. You might perhaps have sinned less if you had asked nothing about Christ, so that, persecuting him only as an unknown man, you would be merely a murderer and would not also appear sacrilegious by offending God. Had you not read how he warns in David's song: "Do not touch my anointed ones, and do my prophets no harm"? Since, then, the divine command must be obeyed, so that neither his anointed nor his prophets suffer any harm from wicked malice, because it is a great crime to treat with insult those consecrated with spiritual ointment, what name will this crime have, that you scheme by your tricks to kill the Lord Christ himself, from whom the anointed take their name, the true Prophet himself, from whom true prophecy comes down? Ought you not to have followed David, who served the Lord's commands? When Saul entered the cave in which David was hiding, and David was urged to kill him, [he answered thus]: "Far be it from me altogether, the Lord forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the Lord's anointed, to lay my hand upon him, for he is the Lord's anointed." And David spared an enemy who wished to kill him; but you lie in wait for the Lord, who was born for the salvation of the world. And if, forgetful of the ancients, you were moved by no examples, you ought at least to have laid down the weapons of your murderous attempt for this reason: so as not to cast down the power of the scepter you bore, you who, though anointed, are found persecuting the author of anointing. Yet, so that the bloody treachery of your name should not leave off before it has had its fill of so great a crime, what you are plotting in your vain rage another Herod will see later: under the heavenly honor of the cross, but through the hellish crime of your nation.

The next passage of the Gospel says: "When they had heard the king, they departed. And behold, the star which they had seen in the east went before them, until it came and stood over the place where the child was. When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy; and entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother, and falling down they worshipped him; and opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense and myrrh." What does it mean that the star they had seen went before them, unless that by following the guidance of a small star they might find the source of full light? And they worshipped, because they had truly come to worship, which Herod, who lied that he would do so, did not deserve to obtain. For none but true worshippers are granted to worship God, as our Lord himself said to the Samaritan woman: "You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews. But the hour is coming, and now is, when the true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth; for the Father seeks such people to worship him." Although the words of the Lord's teaching are clear and plain, that only truth worships God, we must still examine more carefully the force of the saying: "The hour is coming, and now is, when the true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth." I think, according to the understanding which the Lord grants to my littleness, that by indicating the present time, in which he openly showed himself to the world, he said that the Father is worshipped in him. For so he made plain in the words that follow, saying: "He has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son as they honor the Father." And splendidly, after saying "in spirit," he added "and truth," since truth follows those who bear the Spirit of God, while falsehood accompanies the spirit that is alien to him. Another mystery is also revealed in the persons of the wise men: through these Gentiles and foreigners who came to him, our Lord Jesus Christ showed the grace of the law that was to come, because he had already prepared for all nations the way of access to him. For he is known to have declared this both through his prophets and in his own person. Through the prophets he foretold it often, but he explained it by the testimony of David thus: "The Lord said to me: You are my Son, today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession." He called the nations a wonderful inheritance, because through the grace of the new covenant they were being prepared to be won for the Lord. And in his own person, in the Gospel, as the good shepherd, he promised this: "And I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one flock and one shepherd." Nor should we believe that the devotion of the gifts lacked divine purpose. For through these offerings, each fittingly of a different meaning, the power of Christ was openly declared. Let us inquire more closely what the gold that was offered signifies. Without doubt so splendid a material, radiant with the wealth of metallic brilliance, is recorded as having been brought to him as to a king. But in this king too we confess that there is a twofold substance: for Christ both reigns spiritually in heaven and was born in the flesh as King of the Jews. The gift of incense, since that incense was once used for religious offerings, is given to Christ as to God; while myrrh, being suited to the burial of bodies, is offered to him who was to die through human flesh, as an honor for his burial. The very offering of three gifts proclaimed by its number the worship of the catholic faith. For God almighty, who sees present, past and future, who always is, ever was and will be, and is of threefold power in his deity, laid the foundation of all things in the course of those times; and yet all things are always present before his eyes, for he has neither taken on the decline of old age nor the growth of youth, but never ceases to be always the same as he is. For when Moses anxiously asked the lofty name of his power, so that he might announce it to the people of Israel, he declared from the flame of the bush that did not burn up: "I am who I am," and he said: "Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: He who is has sent me to you." Likewise in the Gospel, to the Jews who set Abraham above him in antiquity, he said: "Amen, amen, I say to you, before Abraham came to be, I am." See the difference between the two substances, distinguishing God and man. Of Abraham he said, "before he came to be"; of himself he did not say "I was," but "I am," since it belongs to the Godhead not to have been but to be; for it abides always in living eternity, neither arising from a beginning nor brought to an end. For time comes from God, not God from time.

The words of the reading continue: "And having been warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they went back to their own country by another way." We too, then, should imitate the faithful deeds of the wise men. As they believed a dream, let us now believe what is most plainly before our eyes. We who have been found worthy to worship Christ, discovered by the sign of the cross shining before us, and to offer him from the treasures of our heart the gifts of threefold praise, must no longer return to the prince of this world, the deceiver who once led us astray. Instead, leaving our former path, let us travel the hidden ways of him who guides the steps of those who trust in him to the heavenly homeland.

Next, these events are told in order: "Then Herod, seeing that he had been tricked by the wise men, was angry, and he sent and killed all the boys in Bethlehem and in all its region, from two years old and under, according to the time he had learned from the wise men." So, tricked by the wise men whom he had expected to trick, the wicked king revealed in headlong anger the feelings he had concealed, if it is fitting to call him a king [?], who neither held to godliness nor governed his own passions. Instead, like a most savage and bloodthirsty lion that, if perhaps a tender lamb has been taken from it, turns its wild rage on the whole flock of little blood, and devours, mangles, tears apart and destroys the gentle herd, while the wretched ewes stand at a distance, calling in vain for their young who are already lost, and stir the empty air with their constant bleating, so Herod, goaded by Christ's escape, did not cease from crushing crowds of little ones with his bloody tyranny. For what crime, I ask, does an innocent crowd suffer death? Why do those who have barely been born deserve punishment already? It is madness, not reason, in this bloody king, who, an enemy of the first cries of infancy, set out to commit a countless crime, slaughtered thousands of children, and in a single grief bereaved so many mothers at once. One poor woman tore at the hair streaming over her face, wounding her bared head with the disfigurement of lost locks; another furrowed her cheeks, wet with showers of tears, with savage nails; another beat her breast bloody with hard blows; and an unhappy mother, now no longer a mother, falling over the cold corpse of her only child, poured out an abundance of milk together with blood from the torn veins of her breasts. No one can set out the images of that calamity, so varied and so many, where with different kinds of lament there was no difference of grief. What did you feel, what did your mind intend, no longer a tyrant but a butcher? What roars did you belch out in your fury when, looking down from the height of your citadel at the wounds of innocent little ones, you saw a vast sea of tears gathered in a flood? Yet among the slain infants, who certainly fell but did not perish, Christ, although he was away, could not be absent: for he is always present in the dangers of his saints, and with loving compassion he himself feels the torments inflicted on others' bodies for his sake.

And when, growing in age, he was twelve years old, a number of years which he had taken on from the flesh as he passed through temporal life in the human manner, he showed himself older than the elders in wisdom and a teacher to the teachers in doctrine, so that, as the open interpreter of his own law, he showed, though lesser in age, how great he was.

Not long afterwards (and what delay can there be in times which, fleeting in their swift course, are already departing before they have come?), as the Evangelist indicates, "Jesus himself was about thirty years old, being, as was supposed, the son of Joseph." Most admirably did he reserve both words, "about" and "was supposed," for the Godhead: for just as he seemed to be about thirty years old, although he is eternal, so he was supposed to be the son of Joseph, although he was born of a virgin. Then he came to the waters of the Jordan to be baptized, seeking what he had come to give, to be washed, he who had come to wash. When John the Baptist saw him (John had sensed him while still in his mother's womb, when he lay hidden there, already aware of the coming Christ, and had exercised the gift of prophecy though he could not yet speak), coming forth, as it were, from the temporary silence of his mute father, he began to cry out and say: "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world." When he says "takes away," he shows that Christ does not have what he takes away; he took it, indeed, not to bear it himself but to destroy it. Just as we see the rising of the radiant day suddenly poured over the darkness of blind night, and yet the light does not lose the grace of its splendor through contact with the gloom it shakes off, so the Lord Jesus Christ, taking up the sins of the human race, did not keep them but drove them away. For as fire makes metals bright by burning away their dross, so the good Craftsman cleansed us of original contagion with his own flame. Then, spotless, he entered the waters and washed our filth in himself, having nothing of his own to wash. Finally, purifying the waters themselves by the majesty of his sacred body, he blessed the fame of that stream, which had won the honor of the Lord's baptism. The waves felt the awesome presence of the Godhead: the sea drew back from the shore, the river flowed back to its source. Of these things the prophet sings, describing them thus: "The sea saw and fled; the Jordan turned back. What ails you, O sea, that you fled, and you, O Jordan, that you turned back?"

The text of the Gospel reading then continues: "And when he had been baptized, he came up at once out of the water; and behold, the heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him. And behold, a voice from the heavens, saying: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Let us consider more attentively how great a mystery is revealed in this passage too. As soon as the Lord had been baptized and came up out of the water, the heavens were at once opened. How could they be "at once opened," when heaven is never seen to be closed to Christ, whose home is always above the stars? But I think, as far as his goodness deigns to inspire my understanding, that the heavens were opened at the moment the Lord came up from the water after his baptism so that in his mercy he might teach by his own example that the kingdom of heaven is opened to man, whose likeness he took on, when man has been found worthy to be bathed in the consecration of the spiritual water. And the fact that the Spirit of God came down upon him in the form of a dove shows, through a bird that has no bitterness of gall, how great his goodness, gentleness and simplicity are. And so that no one might fail to know that it was God who had been seen in bodily form, this is affirmed by the voice of the Father, saying: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." This splendid expression of love contains the full firmness of catholic doctrine and declares that the Father and the Son have one power. For the love that exists in God does not depart from the spirit of likeness and equality. He who said in the law of his commandment, "You shall love your neighbor as yourself," taught that there ought to be no distance between the one who loves and the one who is loved. And in the next words he added, "in whom I am well pleased," he is understood to have made plain the shared power of the one Godhead. For to say "I am well pleased" (conplacui) says more than "I am pleased" (placui), since conplacui is a word of agreement and is seen to belong to two persons together. The heavenly voice expressed it so in order to show that the Father is well pleased in the Son and the Son in the Father. Indeed, in this very gathering together of the Father's voice, the Son's baptism and the Spirit's flight, the Trinity shone forth from the one God; and whoever does not reckon it as a unity does not deserve to be found worthy of him.

"Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the desert to be tempted by the devil. And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry. And the tempter came to him and said to him: If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread." So he was tempted by the devil, who is ever the enemy of faith. For no one puts to the test what is plain to him, except one who, full of deceitful cunning, does not believe the truth he has discovered. Such was the devil himself. After he had learned from the clear words of the Father that Jesus was the Son of God, and had been terrified by his unique power in eating nothing for forty days and forty nights (for although Moses and Elijah likewise endured a fast of as many days and nights, the devil knew that they had done so upheld by help from another, however great their own merit, whereas he saw that Jesus was acting by his own power), he suddenly seized on the utterly empty hope of a foolish temptation, because the Lord was hungry. He would not have dared to attack the Godhead had he not seen a man joined with it. At once he set about his ancient snare of food and stirred up his wicked tricks with his usual deceit; and pointing to the stones, which were rather his own fare, the serpent said: "If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread" — as though he could not do this who continually performs just such a work: from the stony bowels of the earth he brings forth crops heavy with wholesome food, and, as nourishment grows from the rock in the thick ears of the harvest, he bestows the rich food of bread out of the fruitfulness of stones. But the matchless Wisdom chose rather to forgo the glory of a wonderful deed, so as not to give room to temptation a second time. For God receives those who believe, but shuts out those who tempt him. We read that the people of Israel offended God above all for this reason: forgetting his benefits, they dared to tempt him, demanding food in their despair. Moses did not pass over their unbelief in silence in his books, and David, recalling it, set it out briefly thus: "They tempted God in their hearts, demanding food for their appetites. And they spoke ill of God and said: Can God prepare a table in the desert?" and so on. For what can be difficult for him who, by reason of his boundless power over all things, is called Almighty? So the Lord answered Satan and said: "It is written: Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God." A most fitting and apt answer was given to the enemy. For when he asked whether he was the Son of God, the Lord answered as a man, so that the devil might be defeated rather by the one he seemed to be attacking. Hearing this, he was broken and weakened, yet he did not lay down the weapons of his boldness. "And the devil led him and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time, and said to him: I will give you all this power and their glory, for they have been handed over to me, and I give them to whomever I wish. If you, then, will worship before me, all will be yours." What wonder if the wretch spoke perversely — he who took on the form of a twisting serpent so as not to walk in straight paths — imagining that Christ could be touched by desire for a frail and perishable kingdom, when he had come rather to bestow a strong and eternal one on his own? Or would he deign to acquire the riches of this world, who had come to teach that they perish? Would he worship a monster cast down from heaven — he whose throne is heaven, whose footstool is the earth, to whom the whole world owes obedience, on whom no one dares to look, and whom all the powers above the stars praise with hushed voices? Again the Lord confounded him with this answer, saying: "It is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve." He is still seen to answer in the person of a man, disdaining, that is, to subdue the feeble rebel by the strength of his greater power. Yet that viperous malice, though thrown down in this encounter of words too, had not yet laid aside its reckless nature, but, trusting in the flicker of its three-forked tongue, raised its wounded head a third time against the victorious hand of the Trinity. "Then the devil took him into the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple and said to him: If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down; for it is written: He has given his angels charge concerning you, and they will bear you up in their hands[, lest you strike your foot against a stone]." Oh, how much blindness and darkness always reigns in a black heart! A mind darkened by the shadows of its own malice does not know how to keep its deceit from being detected. See: by saying "If you are the Son of God," he shows that he does not know it. When he goes on, "He has given his angels charge concerning you," he confesses that the one he sees is indeed that Son. But by using such double-edged and shifting speech he is found out as one who pretends and dissembles, and is proved a liar by his own arts. The wicked heart is the home not of deceit alone but also of folly. For what could be found more absurd than to believe that he would fear a headlong leap from the lofty roof of the temple, however high, and from the top of its towering pinnacle — he who came down from the highest citadel of heaven in order to be seen on the level ground of earth, of whom David cries out: "And he bowed the heavens and came down" — holding the lowest things together while not abandoning the highest? So the divine voice struck down the boldness of the failing foe with these words: "It is written: You shall not tempt the Lord your God." Here, now revealing himself as Lord and God, he forbids the tempter to make any further such attempts. And by his own example our loving teacher reminds us that the spirit who is the craftsman of ancient malice is, without any doubt, made subject to human strength wherever God has been poured into the simplicity of a pure heart.

The instruction of the reading then says: "Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and ministered to him." In this departure of the fleeing devil, and the angels' ministry that followed, I think there is shown in advance, through foreshadowing signs, an image of the glory of Easter. For just as the angels ministered to the Savior once the temptations had been overcome and the devil driven off, so, having made light of the insults and punishments of the Jews by the blessed passion of the cross, and having trampled down death itself, the devil's fruit, Christ rose from the underworld, was carried up to the stars, and is worshipped by the angels in heaven with the sovereign majesty that is his own.

Next he called certain fishermen and joined them to himself as disciples, to fish from then on for human souls, which, pursuing the slippery pleasures of the world, had wandered on aimless courses through voluptuous falls, like swimmers in the uncertain paths of the heaving sea. And he won for eternal life men such as these, whom no noble lineage of earthly birth could puff up and no polish of learned eloquence could exalt with the glory of empty chatter, but whom the holy rule of a simple life, distinguished by a humility that was lofty indeed, made already neighbors of heaven. For Almighty God chose rather what is foolish and weak in the world, rejecting what seems wise and strong, since, as the apostle Paul, that excellent teacher, writes: "The foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men." And straightaway he said again: "God chose what is foolish in this world to shame the wise, and God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong, and God chose what is lowly and despised in the world, and things that are not as though they were, to bring to nothing the things that are." Moreover, the merciful Savior, wishing to bring swift salvation, also laid down the manner of praying and the words of prayer. And the most loving Judge wishes to be asked briefly, so that he may the more quickly grant the petitioner's request. So he taught that we should pray to the Father — his own by nature, ours by grace — bestowing his own honor on human beings, so that the excellence he alone possesses he might grant as a gift to all.

OUR FATHER, WHO ART IN HEAVEN. We who dare to call the everlasting ruler of the heavens by the name of Father must first take note that the gift of so great a favor has been granted not to individuals separately but to all in common. For even if someone, set apart from others and dwelling hidden in some secluded place, calls on the Lord with the words of this prayer, he will not say "My Father" but "Our Father," since that word belongs to Christ alone, whose Father God is in the proper sense. Although this is written throughout all the Gospels, the Lord Jesus himself clearly taught the unique power of his own right, set apart from that shared by the people at large, in the passage where he comforted his disciples, saying: "I am going to my Father and your Father." In saying "my," he fittingly claimed this special glory for himself; in saying "your," he made it plain that a general grace belongs to all in common. And since it is written, "Let earthly things teach you what heavenly things are," let us draw a comparison here, so that we may grasp divine things from human ones. Let us suppose, then, some nobleman who has an only son and a number of servants. Just because he is called the father of the household, can the servants and the son stand on an equal footing in his affection, when the son himself is shown to be master of them all? So it is we who use this prayer, not Christ, since in the petition of this prayer we also call upon him who is one Lord with the Father, coeternal with him. In saying "Our Father," then, we confess that we are all brothers in him. We must not slight the bond of this name by casting out mutual love, nor follow the precedents of that first hatred by which Cain, who shed his brother's blood, became the founder of the stain of kindred murder. Rather, burning with the fire of a gentle spirit, let us lay aside the wickedness of the old fleshly nature and rejoice to be clothed with the new man, so that our earthly deeds may not begin to fall away from heavenly ones and we be seen unworthy of so great a Father, who through Christ has received us, born by holy adoption.

HALLOWED BE YOUR NAME. What hallowing can we conceive of by which the Lord, who hallows all things, could be hallowed, except that we prepare a heart that is devout, gentle, peaceful and chaste for his entering in? Then, delighted with such a dwelling, he may work in us an increase of his own holiness, just as our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who always shone with the bright light of divinity, says that he has been glorified in his disciples. For in the Gospel according to John he prays to the Father for his disciples, and among the various words he spoke he says this: "And I have been glorified in them", because, that is, he found his own glory in them. So where he finds the signs of his own holiness, there he says that he himself is hallowed. For that boundlessly gentle love declares that whatever it makes fruitful in its servants is bestowed on itself. The same meaning is shown when he commands that he be blessed, although it is rather he who blesses all things; for the universal hymn of the three young men singing in the furnace cries out that the Lord is to be blessed by every creature in turn.

YOUR KINGDOM COME. We ask that the kingdom come of the King who never ceases to reign, so that he may punish the deceitful prince of this world for his presumptuous tyranny, and that he alone who alone exists may display his own dominion, which knows no death and cannot be consumed by time. For the day of that light, unbroken by night, knows no time. There the bravest soldier, having worshipped Christ and come out victorious after the many battles of the world, will at last rejoice in the crown of everlasting nobility that is to adorn the hair of his blessed head.

YOUR WILL BE DONE, AS IN HEAVEN, SO ON EARTH. Here too the sense seems to follow on from the preceding petition: we ought to ask with unceasing prayers, day and night, that the will of him who wants wickedness to exist nowhere may fill heaven and earth. Then he will not allow the devil, cast down from heaven, to be hostile to the earth either. Nor will that savage serpent attack the earthly substance of our body, formed as it were from clay, as food for his greed, entangle us in his wicked persuasions, and wrap and coil us in his scaly knots until, intoxicating us with deadly poisons, he licks away our wretched life and devours it. So let us constantly beseech the Lord to guard in us the soul and the flesh alike; for by one part we belong to heaven, by the other we are the seed of earth.

GIVE US TODAY OUR DAILY BREAD. When we ask for the nourishment of daily bread, a threefold meaning opens up, though all the divine Scriptures should be understood in this way. According to the letter, we seem to ask specifically for bread made from grain, so that we may eat; and in the moral sense we pray to the Lord as servants that we may be worthy to receive our daily ration. Yet we must recognize that both of these meanings proceed from spiritual teaching. For this is why we are commanded to ask each day for the food that sustains life: so that by keeping nothing back for tomorrow we may not be seen to doubt God's loving care. Yet this proves so hard and demanding that such a rule can be kept by only a few, and very rare, men. For the Lord himself, faithful in all things, who led the children of Israel out of Egypt and for very many years in the barren desert governed them with daily food, so that they saved food only for the Sabbath, has promised in the words of the Gospel that he will do this for us too, if our faith does not fail. Among other things that he taught, he addressed his disciples thus: "Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself." But if we wish to understand these words more fully in their spiritual sense, we shall see that this bread is the divine word. If the mind is left empty of its substantial teaching and goes hungry even for a little while, it will suffer the want of a great famine. For there is no small difference between spiritual and bodily food. The one we are taught to eat sparingly, the other never to refuse. Here abstinence is healthy; there hunger brings life. Indeed David proclaims in these words that blessedness belongs to those who practise meditation on the Lord's law day [?] and night: "Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence; but his will is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he will meditate day and night." For this meditation satisfies abundantly and delights like the sweetness of thick honey, which, although it quickly fills the stomach of the one who eats it, is yet never found by its nectar-like sweetness to turn nature against it. Let us hear what the same prophet says on this: "How sweet are your words to my throat, O Lord, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!" He made it perfectly clear that the words of the law are to be understood as food when he says that they are sweet to the throat, not to the ears, and that they are served to the mouth more than honey and the honeycomb, not to the hearing. For the deaf too, who have no help from hearing, are filled in the same way with the heavenly precepts as they read them by means of the mouth. And the apostle, writing to the Corinthians, made it plain that spiritual food is teaching when he said: "And I, brothers, could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but as to carnal, as to infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet able." Who, I ask, would doubt or question that all this was meant in a spiritual figure? For not even a fool could suppose that they were infants or had received the nourishment of milk from the apostle. Rather, we should understand that those who are beginning to drink in the words of the law and to be gradually instructed in the divine teachings drink, like infants, the milky first principles; for just as good teaching is wholesome food, so bad teaching is harmful. That is why the Lord warned his disciples to beware above all of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees, knowing that the poison of sour doctrine corrupts, at the slightest touch, the richness of all sweetness; for, as the same apostle Paul says, "a little leaven corrupts the whole lump." And even if we rather believe that this bread is the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, it is nevertheless in no way seen to depart from the spiritual meaning, especially since such a meal and such a prayer are given by God to none of the Gentiles and none of the Jews, but to Christians alone.

AND FORGIVE US OUR DEBTS, AS WE ALSO FORGIVE OUR DEBTORS. If we weigh the request of our petition more carefully, we perceive from our own examples whether pardon is to be granted to us or refused. For we are commanded to hope from the Lord for what we are seen to have forgiven a fellow servant, since the same promise binds us on equal terms: just as we do not want to be debtors, so we should not wish to have debtors. For in the persons of others we are either set free or bound. If anyone thinks it uncertain what debtors are meant here, the grounds for that feeble excuse must be set aside: whether it is perhaps in a fault, or in money, or in anything else that your brother is guilty toward you, let it go. For both our frequent presumption in sinning and our dishonest dealing in sums of money show that we are entangled in very many bonds before God. Whoever, in proportion to the means at his disposal, is inhuman toward the needy denies to God what is his and disowns it; for God's infinite love so protects the distress of the wretched that he testifies that whatever kindly stewardship gives to the poor has been done for himself. In the vows that we make too, once we have obtained God's benefits, we remain debtors until we pay them with a faithful mind. So what has been said of debts of money we should also understand of the other, various kinds of sin by which we are held bound to the eternal judgement, knowing that the comparison with money has been applied to crimes for this reason: that the root of all evils is greed, and without its vicious seed hardly any crimes are born in the world. One man commits murder to snatch from an innocent person what he has coveted; another, enticed by a bribe he has taken, swears to false testimony. Some it drives to pander the traffic of adulterous intercourse for a shameful price; others stain themselves with theft; others deny a deposit entrusted to them. There are many other things like these, in which the hunger for gold always fights as an ally. Hardly any crime is committed without the aid and service of money. Therefore, having obtained the gift of God's love and gained the impunity of heaven's pardon, let us not refuse one another what we have received. Otherwise, set free from greater debts but refusing to release small ones, we shall be bound again in the heaviest chains, and that merciful Lord, a giver and not an exactor of debts, who forgave us ten thousand talents, if he finds us strangling a fellow servant over a hundred denarii, will at once order us handed over to cruel torturers to exact everything; and thrust into the custody of prison we shall not be allowed to come out at all until we repay everything we squandered, down to the last quarter-penny.

AND LEAD US NOT INTO TEMPTATION. This is not because the Lord, who is the way of light and the path of peace, leads anyone into the snares of temptation; but, turning away from those who do not obey the divine warnings, he abandons them and allows them to enter. For all who pursue the slippery contagions of the world, caught in the nets of pleasure, and seek the luxuries of an alluring ruin, are forsaken by the Lord, the lover of pure virtue, and go on to enter wherever the temptation of pleasure has drawn them. Let us therefore strive to draw our foot back from it, treading instead the narrow path, which by a slender track unknown to many climbs unseen to the steep gate of the heavenly kingdom.

BUT DELIVER US FROM EVIL. When we pray to be delivered from evil, we confess that the one we ask to deliver us is good. And rightly is he who delivers to be followed, and he who slaughters to be shunned. For in the one, through good fruits, is the tree of life; in the other, through bad fruits, the root of the ancient transgression. The Gospel reading has made clear that fruits are to be understood as deeds, where the Lord, laying bare the different minds of various people, commanded that each be known by his fruits, that is, by his works, saying: "By their fruits you will know them." Indeed, as far as heaven is separated from earth, fire from water, light from darkness, peace from war, and life no less from the grave, so far, and at so great a remove, are good things distinguished from evil. For a twofold choice always lies open to the decision of our will, whether to keep to the right-hand road or the left, and we are neither ignorant nor uncertain that the right-hand path belongs to the righteous who rejoice in the bosom of the patriarch Abraham, while the left is assigned to the deep torments of the ungodly, from which no one can cross over to the other across so great a chasm and the immense peril of so sheer a gulf. This, then, is the freedom we should long for: that, if we are found worthy to be counted sheep and lambs of the supreme Shepherd, we may deserve to escape the savage bites of the wolf, and in the sweetest pastures of Christ, in the most pleasing loveliness of abundant flowers, may graze now on a life made secure.
BOOK THREE.

The Lord first chose to attend a wedding, and there he gave proofs of his power. As the chief guest, revealing his divine might, he sought not to be fed but to feed. The wine ran out at the festivities, and amid the heaps of food piled on the dishes only the cups, now empty, sat idle in sheer dryness. The earthly drink had gone, so that the heavenly drink might come in. So Christ then changed the waters, and they passed into the appearance of wine. The waters lost what they had been born to be, and now themselves needed water before they could be drunk; the liquid, made nobler than it was born, changed its colour and its name together. Sweet new wine glowed red in everyone's cups, and the guests, captivated by its sweetness, were made drunk on pleasant draughts of river-nectar at every table. The servants who had drawn from the springs were astonished that the six jars they had filled with water were darkened with overflowing wine, and that all of them had suddenly seethed with Christ's vintage. For he who is the vine was present there, fruitful through the tending of his power, nourishing under the shade of heavenly leaves the clusters of the spiritual vine, which will live for ever in delight.

Then a certain royal official tearfully begged the Lord to relieve the affliction of his sick and dying son, and to keep the weak soul from slipping out of its tormented body. Then the generous kindness of divine power, which denies nothing to one who believes and does not hold back its gift by delay, since it never departs from the company of faith, granted the boy full health by a word and bestowed it by speech. For he answered: “Go, your son lives.” How commanding is the Lord's power, and how magnificent! He did not promise that the boy would live, but declared that he was already alive. For this belongs to the Godhead alone: to see as already past whatever it has decreed shall come.

From there he directed his health-bringing steps through various cities and crossroads, through countryside, villages and forts, driving out diseases and healing every limb. Then suddenly, from the midst of the thronging crowd, a leper came up. He was steeped in many kinds of misery, made more wretched by a loathsome whiteness, and he entreated the Lord, saying: “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.” The suppliant showed no small faith in that word, for he believed that his cleansing depended on the divine will alone. As soon as the Lord touched him with his holy hand and said, “I will; be clean,” the two-coloured sickness left at once.
