The body put off the horror of its spotted skin and was free of that alien foulness. The people saw him changed by sudden help. Now that he showed a healthy form, he seemed easier to recognize in his true appearance, though harder to recognize by the colour that had been his.

Peter's mother-in-law was violently stricken by a gasping fever. Her inner parts were seized by fire, and the torch of fierce heat had lodged sharply in her burning marrow. The fate of her trembling soul hung uncertain between death and life, and the excessive flame in her limbs was hastening the arrival of cold death. But when the Lord visited the sick woman, caught up in such danger, with his saving touch, the deadly fire suddenly fled, quenched by a living spring. The woman rose restored and busied herself in diligent service: she who had just been languishing became the servant of her physician.

Moreover, in his mercy he often drove the madness of diabolical savagery out of the limbs of afflicted humanity, so that a spirit that was not divine might not rage when lodged in a divine work. Everywhere, for countless crowds, he restored the use of wounded bodies as diseases fled, and as the danger subsided he rescued whole peoples from all kinds of plague and sickness.

Then, walking along the shore on a sandy path, he boarded the deck of a small boat and began to cross over with his disciples. When the vessel, driven by the swelling sail, was already being carried far from shore, a harsh and cruel storm arose. It stirred the whole sea to its depths with gales; as a wave receded the stern was swamped, and then it was lifted again by swelling waves. Despair of rescue threw the sorrowful disciples into confusion, and even the sailors were forced to admit that their craft offered no remedy at all. In the end all of them believed they were already lost and would be dashed as castaways on the rocky shores, either clinging to the planks and timbers or tumbling along as they swam with their arms. But Christ, the true and provident helmsman, propped on a small pillow, lay peacefully asleep in the tossing stern, asleep in body but wakeful in majesty, since according to David's prophecy, “He who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.” When the disciples cried out with one voice, “Lord, save us, we are perishing,” he rose, roused from sleep. He commanded the winds to be still and ordered the sea to be silent, and suddenly an unexpected calm of sea and sky alike betrayed the divine presence. What then should we think about that storm? Did the sea raise savage gales against the Lord, or did the winds try to stir up a rebellious struggle against their Creator? Far be it from us to think that the elements attempted anything that would insult his majesty! Rather, so that we may recognize that all things are subject to Christ's powers in humble devotion, we believe that the whole sea was overjoyed at the Lord's voyage. It came obediently, rushing up from the lowest depths of the waves and foaming with a whiter surge. So too the swift nature of the light winds spread its wings in winged delight and surrounded the boat in which Christ sat, like a serving throng around the royal camp of a general. For whoever is backed by the licence of violent power is not easily compelled to obey a commanding master; yet the sea and the winds bowed to Christ's divine commands and suddenly laid down their headlong, rushing courses in languid stillness.

Meanwhile the Lord was carried across the now quiet and gentle waters, left the boat and walked along the edge of the nearby shore. Suddenly two most savage men, possessed by a grim legion of demons, leapt out of the tombs with a terrible roar; for this reason they had been bound with iron chains. Alas, how grievous is the condition of madness! Whoever suffers the force of tearing insanity must also be subjected to chains as a punishment. Yet it was fitting that that most wicked spirit, which has nothing in common with life, should dwell among graves and ashes. Then, terrified by the Lord's coming and driven out of the minds he had occupied, now cleansed, he was afraid to ask leave to enter human form again, since he saw that Christ bore that form. So, as he deserved, he obtained leave to go into an animal that delights in unclean filth and is always wrapped in the friendship of stinking mire. Black, shaggy and bristling, he took care to choose a dwelling like his own deformity. At once the grim phalanx charged into the herd of swine, drove it headlong into the waters of the sea and killed it. Not without reason is the devil called the enemy of all, for he is so harmful to everyone that he attacks those he hates and destroys those he loves.

From there the Lord, carried again by the obedient boat, entered the territory of his native soil; because the Creator of all had willed to be born there, he called a town of that region his homeland. Then four men, with a bed on their shoulders, brought him a sick man who was scarcely still a man and already a corpse. His life lacked all bodily movement and was a foretaste of a funeral. His limbs lay there, the bonds of his sinews loosened and slack, and through his flabby, damaged joints, estranged from him by the wasting of disease, they could not perform their proper functions. When the Lord saw that he needed his strength restored by heavenly power, he first took care to absolve him from his sins, which are the roots of all evils, so that once the squalor of filth had been driven out, health might enter the cleansed man as into a house prepared for it. So he said to the man lying there, wretched for the moment but soon to be happy: “Rise, take up your bed and go to your house.” Without delay he rose to obey the command: strong instead of weak, confident instead of despairing, living instead of dying. He took up the little bed on which he had lain motionless, he who had become drier than its hard, dry wood, and walking at last on his own feet he rejoiced to be free of others' footsteps. In grateful repayment, he soon carried back on his own serving shoulders the bed that had carried him.

While the Lord was working these miracles, the daughter of a ruler of the synagogue reached the end of her life and breathed her last. Her body lay motionless, now owed only to burial. Then her father, wounded by the loss of his child, whose death had taken away his already flourishing hope of descendants, came running out and, weeping and groaning, threw himself at the Lord's feet. Barely able to get out his words of prayer through shaking sobs, he said: “Have mercy on a bereaved father, have mercy on a forsaken old man. I have, or rather I had, an only daughter. She has just died, not yet of marriageable age, and she has taken from me the name of father. Bring help and come to our aid; restore her departed soul to limbs that are already growing cold, you who have power over all things and whose power over all things nothing can oppose.” Scarcely had he finished these prayers when the Lord, thronged by disciples and crowds, was already on his way to the dead girl to raise her.

Among the crowds walked a woman who had suffered for twelve years from an excessive flow of blood. She had given much to physicians and gained nothing, and was being drained of her money and her blood alike. But when faithful confidence began to abound in the hidden depths of a heart that believed and was already well, she pushed vigorously into the midst of the crowds, longing to touch at least the small edge of the Lord's garment. Hiding behind him, she suddenly snatched a stolen healing from the outermost edge of the hanging fringe. O how much better it is, when seeking hard things, to trust than to ask! For confidence comes from the heart, prayers from the tongue; prayers are often poured out without the heart, but confidence is never born without it. Look: a woman in despair after the torment of long suffering comes to the physician, not pleading, not groaning, not lamenting, but in silence she carried off what she sought. Silence stood on her mute lips, while her soul cried out to God. Soon a greater flood of faith dried up the streams of surging blood. No one knew of the grace the woman had received, but the gift of his own bounty did not escape Christ, from whose springs had flowed what fulfilled the hope of the trusting woman. He made so faithful a theft public, and rewarded the boldness of the robbery with saving gifts.

Meanwhile they had reached the mourning roof of the wretched house, where the virgin's untimely corpse lay laid out amid everyone's tears. A tearful gathering and uproar had filled the whole place with cries of bitter wailing. The flute-players sounded their groaning tunes, songs to soothe the powers below, and the joyless crowd ran about, loud with repeated grief, throwing the unhappy house into confusion. The Lord forbids them to weep for one who is laid out in sleep, forbids them to mourn as dead one who will live. To all the others the body seemed lifeless; to Christ alone, who had come to give life, she seemed to have fallen asleep. And this belonged to his unique glory, that he called the dead girl sleeping: when he was about to show the parents deeds of wonderful power, he declared that he was giving less than he gave, so as to avoid the harm of human praise. Then, softening with the fire of the spirit the motionless corpse, the body already cold and stiffened in the chill of death, he raised the virgin from the underworld by the authority of his commanding voice, and granted that a girl born once should live twice. The parents stood astonished at their daughter, hesitating to believe what they saw. Moved by the joy of this sudden event, they shed tears more freely for joy and so changed the kind of their weeping.

Departing from there, having performed this work of restored light, he sees two men who had lost their sight and were afflicted, entreating him in words much like these: “Have mercy on us, son of David.” They were asking for the mercy by which he would remove the darkening night and restore day to their extinguished faces. How safe it is to believe, how sound to trust earnestly in God! For they already saw with the heart, who sensed the path of light as Christ walked by. Then the eyes, pressed shut in the suppliants' sorrowful blindness, flashed at the Lord's touch like a sluggish fire when oil is poured on it; and when his bright right hand was laid on them, their faces shone, now seeing, with lamps of their own.

Scarcely had these been sent away when another was brought to him, weak with a threefold disease. Deprived of voice and emptied of hearing, his limbs robbed of their use and left empty, he seemed to be full of nothing but a demon. The Lord cured him at once by reversing these conditions: he emptied him by casting out the demon, and filled him again by pouring back his voice and hearing alike.

Without delay he gave the twelve disciples as much power as his own, commanded them to be able to accomplish everything they had seen him do, and sent them out, rich in every power, to seek the lost sheep, that is, of the house of Israel, since he had not yet spread the dignity of this name throughout all nations. So among his other commands he admonished them thus: “Go and preach, saying, ‘The kingdom of heaven has drawn near.’ Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. Freely you have received, freely give.” It is as if the Lord, anxious with a shepherd's care, were saying: “Since I am the good shepherd, I carefully entrust my flocks to you as skilled workers, and for their sustenance I share fields that belong to me. So let no one sell to my lambs and sheep the pastures that are under my power.” He first handed this down to the apostles' instruction so that from their teaching doctrine might then spread and flow down to later generations, just as we read that four rivers burst forth from the one spring of paradise, and from their courses countless streams branch off and wander to the ends of the whole world. Whoever, then, performs a work of the Godhead, which he does not do as his own but has worthily received through spiritual tradition, has obtained the grace of a free gift; let him be devoted to the grace of a free gift, so that he may appear a steward rather than a merchant, and, fulfilling the song of David's joy, may proclaim for himself the hope of the life to come: “Because I have not known trading, I will enter into the power of the Lord.” For no one, without the Lord's generosity, can have anything to minister or any source from which to distribute gifts, unless he has received what he pays out. Let us hear the apostle Paul saying the same: “Let a person regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Now it is required of stewards that one be found faithful.” And again the same teacher warns and says: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if

you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?” Then, when the Lord had entered the synagogue, he saw a feeble man, crippled by numbness in part of his body, half-dead in his afflicted limbs, wholly neither living nor dying. The ice of sluggish torpor had cut off his withered right hand, and it was now past all hope of use. Then, with powerful and commanding help, he caused the hand, estranged from him by its idle sinews, to be quickened by the movement of the veins into the warmth of blood. He did not do it by skill but granted it by command, saying: “Stretch out your hand.” And he stretched out his hand, and it was restored to him like the other. Truly this gift of God is unique, and he exercises it without ceasing, for he takes nothing away from human well-being and always restores all things.

Look, that slippery water-snake is here again, that harmful reviver of the tricks of his old arts. Swelling with the livid venom of his gall, he delights to grow fat on human gore. The poison he had often poured out on many people, each seized by a different suffering, he now heaped up in his rage on the limbs of one man: he snatched away his mind, shut up his voice and extinguished his light, and binding three disasters together at once, he drove a mute and blind man to madness. To him the merciful Saviour of the whole world, our light, the Word of the Father, drove out the foul spirit, restored his sight and changed his mouth. Through the Word words come forth; through the Light the eyes' lights revive.

A woman too had come to be healed, bent more by an old disease than by old age. She trembled as she moved, gasped with groans, was curved at the shoulders, her face bowed down, always looking down, stooped and depressed, at the lowly earth. Raised up by the Lord's powers after eighteen unbroken years, her limbs straightened and lifted, she gazes at the sky and the stars and remembers that she once saw the burning globe of the sun. You who worship idols, consider the difference between God, whom you flee, and the demon, whom you appease, if indeed one who never ceases to do harm can be appeased. For all whom he possesses are oppressed, while those whom Christ loads with the yoke of sweetest lightness are lifted up.

Then, like Moses whom he prefigured, and as the true prophet, he saw that the people who had followed him into the desert were fainting, overcome by the barrenness of the place, as of old, and he renewed the ancient comforts with most wonderful increase. For then he made the flesh of many birds suddenly appear; now he made the quantity of two fish overflow. Then he poured abundant manna from heaven; now, distributing five loaves, he provided an abundant feast for as many thousands of men. The number of the rest of the crowd went unrecorded, for the multitude of women and little children had no count. And what you will marvel at still more, whoever reads this, if you are learning it for the first time: after the hunger of the people had been driven away and they were satisfied, the mass of fragments that was gathered up filled twelve baskets. The abundance was not as great when it was given out as it was in the leftovers, which no one wanted any more, when they were gathered up.

Meanwhile, as the ocean received the sinking day under the dark-blue heat of its surging waves, and pale evening announced the approach of starry night, the Master stayed on land and the disciples alone set out by boat across the sea, and the sea raged against the vessel, exposed as it was to contrary winds. Then, about the fourth watch of the shadowy night, the Lord came walking on the waves he trod, pressing down with gentle steps the swollen billows of the foaming deep, and the sea licked Christ's sacred footsteps with mild washing. The men in peril marvelled at the sudden, new sight: paths for ships had opened up as a road for a man on foot. While all wavered whether it was truly the Lord appearing, or whether uncertain phantoms of darkness were deceiving eyes clouded by fear of danger, Peter, the companion and friend of faith, to whom an intimate grace always granted to recognize Christ, asked to come to him. Called, he went down into the sea without trembling and was not swallowed by the greedy flowing waves, since, held up by the help of the Lord's hand, he had taken refuge in the safest harbour of that mighty right hand. He cut a path across the glassy plains of the salt sea's marble, a traveller on foot against the very nature of the sea. O growth of increasing faith! Earlier he had scorned his nets, the livelihood of a poor man; now he spurned life itself, so that he might come to Christ.

So the Lord left the boat and walked the land of Gennesaret with the company of his disciples. Its inhabitants gladly welcomed his arrival and brought together their people who were burdened with various illnesses into his divine presence to be healed, so that by touching even the fringe of his garment they might be cured of the harshest diseases. And whoever was worthy to obtain this was soon restored to health. How precious was this garment! Or rather, it had no price: sold in no trade, it itself redeemed everyone by the gifts of a little thread.

From there, as he passed along the roads of the region of Tyre and Sidon, a Canaanite woman, distressed by her daughter's affliction, for a black spirit had taken possession of her, humbly entreated him. She asked to be counted equal to the dogs, which shrewdly never leave their masters' tables, so that by licking up the scraps shaken off they may feed on the meagre crumbs that fall. A most humble voice, but a lofty faith! Her daughter was restored, and her faith soon changed the dog into a sheep; she who had sprung up among the thorns of her own people it brought into the pastures of Hebrew grass.

Then, climbing the high ridges of a mountain, accompanied by countless people, he restored to their former use thousands of the lame and the blind alike, the deaf too and lepers who had gathered there, those whose hands were weak, and whatever sick folk had streamed together. He set the organs of their feeble limbs in good order, with their own sinews and their own movement.

While by the working of his wonderful power he was restoring the stricken throng, the third day was passing. In those barren, parched places the weary people had touched no food at all, and their faint hunger was nursing a trouble that would only be made worse by a double labour, if the exhausted people had to bear the long burden of want, growing heavier as they retraced their steps along the road. Moved by compassion for this, the Almighty, who is always the generous bread of the needy and gives food where barren necessity has denied crops, with a very few small fish and seven loaves broken into pieces satisfied four thousand men, besides an immense crowd of women and a swarm of little children like bees. And so that you may marvel at something even greater, the food increased while it was being eaten, and the fruitful losses at the tables produced food nourished by the very bites. Hunger, put to flight, was terrified at its own leftovers heaped up in seven baskets, when so great an abundance of fragments was gathered and it saw a manifold harvest overflowing from a little seed.

Although from the moment of his birth from his mother Christ appeared to bear the mortal limbs of a human body, he could not conceal that he was God. For a city set on the top of a mountain is not hidden, nor is a burning lamp put under a hollow bushel; it is raised higher, and the substance of its living flame gives light to all. So he led three disciples with him as witnesses up to the heights of a mountain, and there, transfigured, he showed them the appearance of his glory: his face shone fiery like the sun, and his garments matched the whiteness of snow. Why the most wise evangelist compared the most brilliant radiance of the divine majesty, which no one's sight can look upon, to the visible forms of the sun and the snow, a plainer explanation will show. There is nothing in this world brighter than the sun or whiter than snow, and he judged that these were to be compared to the supreme Godhead because nothing beyond them is granted to mortal eyes. Yet that surpassing brilliance of the Lord so outdid both the sun and the snow that, while anyone's gaze can easily look at the sun and the snow, the apostles could not look upon Christ shining in the brightness of his own light, and they fell with their faces to the ground. O lofty summit of exalted merit, to which it was given to know in the world what the world did not deserve to perceive! What of the fact that they also recognized Elijah and Moses, whom bodily sight had never known, with their inner eyes, so that the truth of a greater faith might become known and show that he is Alpha and Omega [?], that is, the beginning and the end? Such prophets were seen to come to him: one of them still enjoys a living old age, while the other reached the goal of final light that no course of human life can pass beyond. And by the oracle of a heavenly utterance sent forth from the sky, saying, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased," the Father's voice taught in words that Christ was his begotten Son.

After the Lord had taken on his bodily appearance again, veiled his heavenly form once more with the covering of flesh, and shown himself openly to the people, suddenly a lowly man, bowed on his knees and cast down with grief, made this plea: "Lord, I have one son left, if he can be called left at all, hanging as he does on the border between death and life. An unclean spirit overpowers him cruelly; it tears at him and keeps trying either to burn him in fire or to drown him in the water that torments him, and after wearing him out with many dangers it is plotting his final end. Drive out this madness from his mind, I beg you, and give him back to me, or rather to himself, so that this blind power, hostile to the light, may not take away the poor boy's despairing life." While he was still pouring out these words with tears and groans, the Lord in his compassion was already making the boy well. Then the raging, turbulent robber, which had long harassed the dwelling that belonged to another and had abused it, being about to depart from the house it had invaded, was stirred into burning wrath. But since, at the Lord's prohibition, it had no power to tear apart the limbs it had seized, it flew off to the underworld and left the boy unharmed.

The King, too, who alone is King of kings and is shown to be Lord of lords, did not disdain to pay Caesar's tax. He commanded Peter, who was fishing, to draw up from the sea's waves a swimming creature that carried a golden didrachma. Then that swift dweller of the restless waves swallowed the quivering snare of the deceiving hook and was hauled out of its native waters by the lashing rod; and that most worthless fish, bearing a rich payment, was worth more for the honor of a weight not its own than for its own. How greatly, too, by this deed Christ wished us to be imitators of his teaching! Though he could have refused the unjust affront of this payment (since he had nothing in common with the people, except to help all with saving benefits), he preferred to pay a charge he did not owe rather than refuse anything to anyone who asked, so that he, the founder and teacher of righteousness, who said, "Give to everyone who asks of you," might be the first to fulfill the precepts of his own law.

And when the apostles, in their usual simple way, asked him who could be counted greater in the kingdom of heaven, he answered as God and as a wonderful teacher. The humble person, he said, is superior to all, and whoever has made himself the last of all surpasses everyone, like the little child whom he held standing in their midst as a spiritual example. He was teaching them to follow the disposition of that small and tender age, not the age itself, since the years of early childhood, in their tiny smallness, have no love for worldly pomp, are not touched by the ambition for honour, and are not puffed up by swelling pride. So the simplicity of a life bent low comes as near to heaven as it comes to the ground. The mind that bows down is raised up, and once it raises itself up it falls away; and the heart's lowlier path, by which it strives to go down, is lifted on high. For God raises the humble and the poor from the dunghill and joins them to the company of the mighty, but the neck of the devil's pride he threw headlong from its heavenly rank into the depths of the filth of Tartarus. For this is what the divine reading declares: "God gives grace to the humble, but resists the proud." And again, recalling the same thing, it says: "He lifts up the needy from the earth and raises the poor from the dunghill, to set him with the princes of his people." For all poverty is the companion of humility. Hear Solomon saying: "Poverty humbles a man." But what we report is far too small and slight if we run through the works of the Godhead one by one and recount them individually, for they are known in general but cannot be unfolded by any words.
BOOK FOUR

And now, crossing the streams of the Jordan once more as he passed along the road through Judea, he healed a vast crowd everywhere, and countless throngs suffering from every nameless kind of sickness, receiving the sick and letting them go home in health. For the supreme God nothing is hard to bestow on those who hope in him, for his power readily suffices to level the steep and straighten the crooked: that is, to bring the proud down to lowlier things and to show the path to those who stray. The great prophet Isaiah is known to have spoken this way when he announced the coming of Christ: "And the crooked shall become straight, and the rough places level roads." Was he prophesying about rocks or thorns or the winding bends of roads, when Christ came to save a world that is set not in forests and mountains but in the human race? This is also what the voice of one crying in the wilderness urges: "Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight". It means the way of our thoughts and the paths of our wills, by which the Lord may walk with a straight step into the dwelling of a pure heart. For thoughts and wills are the ways of works, which are seen to go before anyone's good or evil deed. Whatever natural strength denies, then, lies most easily within the reach of divine power.

For just as the camel, a huge beast, cannot pass through the tiny eye of a needle because of the bulk of so large a body, so the opulent, swollen rich man could not enter the heavenly kingdom through the slender gate of the narrow path. That would be so had not the provident Governor of all things consoled the disciples who were troubled by this condition with such words as these: "With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible." He holds the whole universe by his law and is not himself held under law; no face ever looks upon him, but he always watches over all things. Not every rich man is weighed down by the inheritance of his wealth, but only the one who is a bad steward of his own abundance. For when the Lord says through the prophet, "The gold and the silver are mine," he shows that what is his is not evil if a good workman holds it. Spending nothing on good works is no different from pouring out a great deal on wicked ones. The man who keeps his wealth safe and lays it up is the one who hides and stores his treasures in heaven, where no bite of devouring moth or scaly rust consumes anything and no breach is dug open for thieves to steal. He supplies food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty and hospitality to strangers. He consoles the sorrowful in prison and cares for those sick in body, and while he is most generous to all, he is poor and needy only toward himself. Nor should anyone doubt that the wealth shown to have been spent on Christ, under the lowliest form of a poor man, will certainly reach heaven. It is increased by losses and preserved by being scattered; it perishes so that it may remain, and though dead it brings back life.

Meanwhile, as the Lord was going out from Jericho surrounded by an accompanying crowd, he saw two men deprived of sight sitting by the roadside bank and begging to have their sight restored. They made their request sitting down, because the hostile darkness kept them from trusting their steps to movement. That power which denies nothing to devotion, and which is accustomed to bring salvation wherever it senses faith burning, did not delay even a little. With a sudden, wakeful touch it roused the eyes pressed shut in long sleep, and, unbarring the bolts of the windows hidden beneath the brow, it let the day in at once and drove back the murky night.
Then, walking once more within the sacred walls of the temple, he gave sight to the blind and restored the lame to walking.

After these monuments of noble miracles he left the city of David and came to the region of Bethany, and returning on the following day he was again making his way to the houses of that city. Not far from the road stood a fig tree, shady with its interwoven covering of leaves. When the Lord, hungry in the flesh, found no fruit at all on its wood, he did not wound the inhospitable branches of the tree with a curse but condemned them with a command, rebuking it thus: "May no fruit ever grow from you again." At once the fig tree, robbed of its sap, became barren and unsightly, laid aside the glory of its foliage, and withered away. Yet we should not take these things literally, even though they are believed to have plainly taken place, since the divine law accords with spiritual meanings. For what sin had senseless matter committed? Especially a tree which, as Mark the evangelist records, had no fruit because it was not the season. The only explanation is that the Lord did this to instruct us for our benefit, since by parables of deeds and words he shows us the way of life. Every effort of human conduct, then, which strives to nourish nothing pleasing to God will be counted as wood for burning, like a useless tree with a sluggish trunk, full of leaves but not of fruit. So too with that fig tree which stood fruitless: the lord of the vineyard who had planted it ordered it cut down, but granted it a truce of one year, so that it might remain if it bore fruit even late; otherwise it would then rightly perish. But it is as the song of the psalm says: "The righteous will flourish like the palm, and like the cedar that is in Lebanon he will be multiplied."

Next a man was brought to him who, besides the affliction of madness, also suffered the loss of speech. The passages of his throat were blocked, so that no voice sounded from the cymbals of his lips, and announcing nothing at all with his mouth, he proclaimed his dumb madness by his silence. But that starry Creator, accustomed to strengthening the weak, shook off the robber who was besieging his throat and pressing on him with gasping constrictions. Through the opened paths of the voice he restored to the tongue, now loosed from its bonds, the full exchange of speech with eloquent freedom.

Moreover, while the Lord was honouring by his own humility the banquet of a certain Pharisee who had invited him, a notorious sinful woman came in hastily. Wounded by the many wounds of her offences, she was leading a shameful life. She fell prostrate at the Lord's feet and did not cease to wash them with her weeping, to wipe them with her hair, and to kiss them and anoint them with precious ointment. At last God pronounced his sentence; he never regrets giving a hand to the fallen, if we repent of the slippery path of our former ruin. He released her in pardon with these words, saying: "Your faith has saved you; go in peace." O how greatly it helps the wretched sick to uncover by confession what becomes deadly when it is hidden! For whoever conceals his wounds nourishes them, and fails to lay bare to the physician the sore in which the goad of pain is lodged. See now: a woman polluted by the contagion of a long-standing disease is purged by the affliction of a little groaning and washed in the flood of her own weeping. Bathed in tears and wiped with hair, she who had come defiled goes away clean.

The Lord also came to the city named Capernaum and was teaching the people heavenly things in a very large gathering in the synagogue. Suddenly that most wicked devil, through the bodily service of a human voice, roared out this cry: "What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are, the Holy One of God." Soon the Lord said threateningly, "Be silent and come out of the man, unclean spirit," and the devil, thoroughly terrified and cast down, left the human breast with a great bellowing roar, by which he confessed that he had been scourged by the divine command, and fled unseen into the dark air. Likewise the Lord brought saving help to many who were sick in various ways and troubled by the calamity of diverse plagues. Many demons were driven out by the word of his power, and he did not allow them to speak at all, disdaining so common a witness to faith in his heavenly majesty. For that ancient serpent of hell, the destroyer of life and inventor of death, had been cast down from the summit of heaven with all the madness of his allied pomp and the whole foul retinue of his damned army. Now he was amazed to see on earth, clothed in the lowliness of the flesh, Christ, whom he had known in starry glory in that citadel. And he groaned the more, livid with envy, because he saw that man was so beloved by the Lord of power.

Then, passing through the region of Tyre, the Lord was walking along the shore of Sidon, and he healed a man brought to him who was utterly wretched with a twofold calamity. Deprived of the use of voice and ears, he could neither give his own words nor receive the words of others. But at the touch of the heavenly hand, all the inner passages that violent ruin had shut were suddenly broken open and the doors flew wide at the push. As the guards of the veins were at once released, he who a moment ago had seemed mute and deaf was granted both to speak himself and to hear others speaking.
You too felt the gifts of the Lord's power, you whose eyes had been pressed shut by hellish blindness. Christ spat on them, and at once the semblance

of a feigned death he wiped away. Teaching the peoples by sacred precepts to secure the support of everlasting life, he was revealing himself more plainly as God. To escape for a little while the crowds pouring headlong upon him, he came to the lake with its sea-like waters, and sitting in Simon's small boat he instructed with divine oracles the people who remained on the shore. At last, when he had finished his words, words that were never too many for their desires, he ordered that the boat put out into deeper water and the fishing nets be let down into the sea. Through the whole course of the night those nets, their labour frustrated, had been able to draw nothing from the depths. Simon gladly obeyed the sacred command. Skilled in enclosing the sea-wandering throngs with a siege of line, he captured the peoples of the watery marble, surrounded as if by city walls. So great a multitude of fish filled the stretched-out folds of the nets that both Simon's boat and the one standing by as its partner, laden with scaly masses, were barely rescued from danger. So too we are often disturbed by the unexpected good fortune of very great success. Even the joy we receive in answer to our prayers, if it goes beyond limit and measure, we come to fear as an intolerable burden, because men are afraid to grant, or even to wish for, what is easy for divinity.

Famous and renowned for such miracles, the Lord, surrounded by disciples and crowds, was hastening to enter the city called Nain. Suddenly he saw the corpse of a young man being carried out, raised high in the sad service of the empty offices of a funeral. Envious fate had long before widowed his mother of her husband, and now, by the misery of a second urn, of her son. Compassion, the enemy of grief, did not delay at all but at once lent its life-giving help, and touching the bier with the hand of redemption, the Lord said to the dead man: "Young man, I say to you, arise." And he who was dead sat up and began to speak, and he gave him to his mother. For though the young man had been deprived of light and overwhelmed by the torpor of sluggish death, and was being carried out as a lifeless corpse, the servant could not keep silent when his Lord called him, nor could the spirit fail to return when Life itself was present. Soon, then, the whole gathering, which had been clouded with weeping, recovered a serene face. Laying aside their grief and turning their steps back along the way they had come, they brought the rejoicing mother back to her home in a bright procession.

Nor was the salvation conferred on you, Mary, by the Lord's healing a slight one. It healed the secret depths of your breast, injured by many blows and wounds, which a sevenfold frenzy, massed in a demonic band, held in its possession with seven assaults of arms. But the serpent, mottled with scaly splendour, fled the dread commands of the Almighty and, driven from your heart, sought the chaos of hellish Tartarus, twisting the coils of its seven members and vanishing in seven folds at once.

Then, so that the rich growth of a plentiful harvest should not languish for want of labourers, who were few, he also sent out seventy-two other disciples. They were simple in mind and shining with purity, and conspicuous in number and merit, they deserve to be called a pound of gold. He ordered them to go like innocent and gentle lambs to the harsh minds of men, as if among ravening wolves. He exhorted them with these words, addressing them: "Go; behold, I send you out as lambs among wolves." And again, when they returned eagerly because even the demons were subject to them, he admonished them, saying: "Behold, I give you power to tread on serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing will harm you. Nevertheless, do not rejoice that the spirits are subject to you; but rejoice that your names are written in heaven." For this is the rule of divine judgment: to set life before deeds, not to prefer deeds to life. If the merit of holy conduct is lacking, miracles carry no weight, for it is proved that they are often displayed even by the wicked. To such people the witness of secrets and judge of deeds foretold in the words of the gospel that he would say at the time of recompense: "I do not know you; depart from me, all you who work iniquity." Such were the two craftsmen of a criminal partnership who once appeared under the Egyptian tyranny of Pharaoh. Trusting in the vanities of Memphis, they strove to rival the heavenly miracles of Moses, and against them they set up rival images and shapes fashioned by magic tricks and human effort.

Meanwhile, at the entreaty of a certain ruler of the Pharisees, he came to a meal, hastening not so much for the sake of eating as to bring glory to his house. There he saw a man distended with the swelling of a false stoutness. His belly was so transparent with overflowing water that it seemed a wineskin rather than a womb, and the monstrous pregnant skin was in labour with an enclosed death. As his limbs wasted away, the immoderate cavity grew, so that emaciation reigned everywhere and had gathered the whole dropsy into the swollen belly. The Father of the world would not allow this sight to remain in his presence. Hastening to heal the man, whom he desires all the more to be his own, he paid no heed to his own sabbath, which had then come. For God did not make man for the sake of the sabbath, as the Lord himself taught with his own words in another chapter of the holy gospel, but brought forth the sabbath for the sake of man. Then, bestowing the work of salvation, he ordered the moist flood in the man's bowels to dry up. Suddenly the diseased water of the bodily marsh departed, and the lake of flesh, which had become glassy, was drained and emptied all at once as the watery plague left it.

When the Lord, making for Jerusalem, was passing through Samaria, Galilee and Jericho, he graciously entered a certain village. Ten wretched lepers saw him from afar. They were utterly loathsome with the spotted foulness of their bodies, for a mottled punishment spread over their faces had made them monstrous with shameful deformity. Together, with one voice, they cried out tearfully: "Jesus, Master, have mercy on us." Then that singular power, which is never empty of compassion, answered mercifully and said: "Go, show yourselves to the priests." Suddenly, as they hurried off, all the blight fled from their limbs, and looking at one another they rejoiced alike in each other's cleansing, because in none of them did anything of the horrible blotches remain. One of them, as if to offer a tithe of the gift received on behalf of all, came back in grateful haste and threw himself on his face before the Lord. Great was the man's faith and great his prudence, for by a single act he paid the debt of a twofold devotion. He showed faith in believing that he had been cleansed by the one he had asked, and prudence in choosing to worship Jesus, though he had been ordered to show himself to the priests. For who but the Lord Christ is the high priest of high priests and the priest of priests? He is the author and founder of the twofold offering. After the order of Melchizedek, the gifts of his own body and blood, which he offered for us when crucified, are offered to him: the sweet food of the wheat harvest and the lovely drink of the pleasant vine.

The son of Timaeus, robbed of light, was sitting beside the road along which he had learned that Christ was passing. Shouting out again and again, he would not fall silent though the people forbade him, but begged more and more to be given the abundant brightness of sight. He was told to come to the Lord, went led by another's hand, and, having received what he prayed for, returned with no guide to support him. O power of unbroken confidence! How forcibly you obtain what you desire! Gathering constant prayers from the heart, you demand it as though it were owed, and so you deserve what you ask. Whatever a harder case denies because of its difficulty, the frequent prayer of a suppliant alone obtains through simple and honest petitions. This is not because anything is difficult for God, but because the magnitude of the matter is beyond human hope. So it was with the man who, in the silence of the night, asked for loaves from a friend who long refused him: since he could not obtain them by the right of charity, he wrested them out with the help of importunity.

As the Lord was also passing through the region of Samaria, he had come to feel the heat of human thirst on a sweltering day. The fountain ever living and always flowing with perennial water desired a little water to drink, insofar as he bore the substance of a body. Here a woman native to that region was drawing water from the deep well. While she hesitated to give him the gift of a little water, she recognized from his prophetic voice the guilt of her own life with many husbands, or with another woman's. She begged the Lord to give her such streams that, since their supply would never fail, her thirst might fail and be done away with. She was wholly ignorant and unaware that no one will possess so great a gift except one who has been plunged in the flood of Jesus Christ and satisfied with spiritual waters in soul, not in body.

While the Saviour, thundering with the Father's voice, was sitting within the walls of the holy temple, he took pity on the wandering people and was turning them to the right path with the friendly counsel of life. Then, all at once, a shameless adulteress was led headlong to him, dragged along by a large gathering of people, to be overwhelmed by blows of stones according to the ordinance of lawful custom. The cruel fury of her accusers thrust her before the merciful judge, wanting him to condemn her, but he set her free. For when the condition was laid down that the one to carry out the punishment of the crime must be one who had no crime of his own, no one was found pure in his own judgment to strike the impure woman. No one dared to pluck the speck from another's eye when he knew that a beam remained in his own. Soon, then, the whole fire of rabid uproar fled, quenched by a flood of conscience, and every accuser was found guilty, confessing it by his silence. Then the clement and gentle sentence of the Lord did not acquit the adulteress of her manifest crime by a verdict, but in mercy did not punish her, on the understanding that she would return to punishment if she returned to her fault. For whoever, in the filthy manner of a dog, seeks out and licks up again what he has vomited cares to keep neither the old pardon nor the future one. He loses the gain of the one, which he acquired in vain, and feels the loss of the other, which he did not deserve to reach.

Departing from this region too, the Lord saw a man blind from birth, who, slipping from the womb of a wretched mother and more wretched himself, came into the light without light. Then that Sower of the human beginning, the Founder and Perfecter of the world, would not allow the fabric of his work to remain incomplete for lack of the material for seeing. He smeared mud, a natural instrument indeed, on the closed barriers of the cheeks, and like a good craftsman he supplied from the old mortar what he had seen to be lacking in the man. Yet the man did not receive sight until, instructed by the Lord's commands, he had come to the healing water of Siloam and, made safe now by the remedy of kindred clay, had washed his eyes in the water poured over them. Soon, then, twin eyes shone out from his healed face, worthy at last to behold the day they had never known before. All who read these things spiritually, therefore, should notice what the mystical miracles of this deed teach. For we are a blind progeny, born of the offspring of most wretched Eve, walking in long wanderings through the darkness of inborn gloom. But after God deigned to take the likeness of human flesh, a saving earth was given to us from the Virgin. Washed in the fountains of holy baptism, it opened our eyes to a reborn brightness.

Then, full of concern, he graciously came with saving steps to Bethany, where Lazarus, having met his end according to the human condition, lay beneath the stone of the tomb, already stinking in the course of the fourth day. When the Lord came to his tomb, the sisters who had gathered there were weeping with dutiful grief, the crowd standing by was weeping, and the Almighty himself wept with them. He wept not in his divinity but in his body, grieving over the cold limbs of the lifeless man in that part in which he himself was to die. For he shed tears as a friend, and showed the glory of his majesty as God. Why, Martha, do you still not believe? And you, Mary, why do you groan? You hesitate in doubtful trepidation over whether Christ can raise one man from the dead, though he will make the countless throngs of the whole world rise again with renewed life. So when the Lord, by the wondrous command of his imperious voice, cried out, "Lazarus, come forth," Tartarus suddenly lay open, shaken with great dread. The inner chamber of hell trembled, the deadly chaos quaked, and the law of deep death withdrew. The soul was poured again into the fibres of its body, the tomb's defences were broken, and the corpse was seen standing alive. After the due rites, after the funeral and burial had been completed, it was as though he had been born and created anew: having died to himself, he became, as it were, his own posthumous child, and walked away as his own survivor.

And so that the Lord, scorning the perishable things of worldly ambition, might show himself the most high God all the more by humility, he did not make his way borne up on lofty chariots at the speed of a four-horse team, with the wheel furrowing the dusty road, for that is a display of love for mortal pomp. Nor did he press the high back of a snorting horse, which, conspicuous in trappings and purple, tosses its restless mouth as it champs the foaming weight of blood-stained gold. Rather, the slow carriage of a most lowly little donkey was honour enough for the Lord. Its hoof, great not in price but through the merit of so great a rider, shone the nobler under that light [?]. It was not unequal to that ancient beast which, though it saw Christ in a humble manger, still recognized that he was God. The grace of this beast of burden shone forth, and as it walked along the middle of the road all the people spread their garments beneath it. Tell me now, all you peoples who until now have lain subject to pagan errors: what reigning king ever had glory like this? Whom did a thronging crowd, in the fullness of festival, ever go out to meet with palms and branches, singing a song of heavenly hymns, except the Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father governs the starry realm, the everlasting Prince in the Prince?
BOOK FIVE

Amid this endless abundance of divine [?] miracles, the Passover was already drawing near, at which the glorious power of Christ chose to lay down his mortal flesh, to take it up again, now living forever. It was not another flesh but the same, which he filled with the reward of light, raised from the underworld and lifted up to the stars. Troubled a little, as a man dreading the approach of death, he cried out to the Father in words of trust and holy devotion, showing himself to be the Son of God: “Father, save me from this hour; but it was for this that I came to this hour. Father, glorify your name.” He spoke in a truly divine and powerful way: when he asked to be glorified himself, he indicated that it was the Father's name that must be glorified. For his name is God, a name the Father and the Son possess undivided, sharing one majesty equally. And a voice came from heaven: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.” What could be plainer than this fulfilled testimony of the Father's declaration? What could be clearer than this oracle of heavenly assertion? Yet the faithless Jewish nation, which had heard the weight of so great a truth, was in no way moved by such manifest signs to believe that the divinity of the Lord Jesus Christ had been proven. Some insisted that it had been a clap of thunder; others argued that an angel had spoken to him. O people truly blind in eye and hardest of heart, of whom Isaiah spoke in prophecy: “He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they may not see with their eyes and understand with their heart and turn, and I heal them.” For it was not thunder, nor an angel, a creature, that begot Christ, its own maker, so as to answer him at once as a father when he called confidently on the Father. No, the voice that replied came forth from the mouth of God, specifically of the Father, who truly knows the Son, so that, at least for this reason, the crowd, utterly unbelieving, might be stung to the heart and led, however late, to heavenly faith. So this is what it means for the Father to answer the Son: to sound in harmony with his own voice. For Christ, begotten of the Word, is the Word of the Father, and the matching exchange of speech revealed the Father in the Son and revealed the Son in the Father.

Then, at the sacred rite of the yearly banquet, while he was celebrating the Passover feast according to custom, he rose and girded himself with a linen towel, so as to teach by his own example above all that humility is to be loved. The Lord, the teacher, bent down before his disciples and washed his servants' feet, and he laid aside the height of his power so completely that he did not exclude even Judas from the honor of this service, though he knew him to be the author of an unspeakable betrayal. But you were to gain no glory from this, accursed traitor, appearing clean in your feet while you were defiled in your soul, like a tomb whitewashed on the outside that is filled within with the horrible filth of corpses. Nor was the plotted treachery hidden from the Lord. He marked out the man who would be the head of the crime as the one to whom he handed bread, he who is himself the Bread that was to be handed over to death. Then the word of David was made plain, which says: “He who ate my bread has heightened his treachery against me.”

After the Lord Jesus Christ had consecrated the two gifts of life, his body and his blood, and had offered his own disciples the spiritual food and drink by which faithful souls, filled with the heavenly banquet, can no longer feel hunger or thirst, the monstrous evil spirit soon entered the heart of Judas, the most wicked dwelling, where it had found envy. Seizing accursed weapons against the Lord, Judas stirred up the madness of a slave's war, having bargained the enormous crime of that deal for whatever sum of payment. For guilt does not lie in the price; the crime grows strong in the deed. Blind man, in taking the small reward of thirty pieces of silver he committed as great a sacrilege as he would have perpetrated if he had gained all the kingdoms of the earth together, the riches of the sea, and the whole region of the sky with its wandering clouds. For all the goods of the whole world could not be compared with the poured-out blood of Christ, who is the father [?] of the entire world and who allowed even this wicked man to be born. Would that he had been condemned by the dry barrenness of his mother and had never seen his birthday nor looked on the pleasant things of the heavenly light, remaining nothing in eternal numbness! It would have been a better lot for the wretch never to know the life that was given him than to feel it taken away. Or, as soon as he deserved to be begotten, would that he had deserved to die as well and had become an example of the first psalm, perishing altogether from the world like the dust that the wind drives from the face of the earth, the unhappy man leaving no memory of his name! Is it then, you bold, bloody, ferocious, rebellious, mad man, you deceitful, cruel, unjust, venal and faithless one, you traitor, robber, savage, betrayer, pitiless and impious, is it then that you go ahead as guide and standard-bearer, accompanying a dreadful enemy? While you menacingly lead a sacrilegious troop violently armed with swords and clubs, do you violate the covenant with lying kisses, mix honey with poisons, and flatter the Lord with a cruel betrayal? Why do you falsely profess yourself his companion and perform the greeting of a friendly fraud? Peace never conspires with harmful swords, nor does a wolf offer savage kisses to the gentlest lamb.

So the holy worker of miracles, though handed over to accursed men, did not abandon his customary help. The servant's ear had been violently cut off by Peter's sword, and so that the merciful one might never at any moment hold back from mercy, he immediately restored and healed it. For it was not fitting that human vengeance should come to the aid of God, who could have asked his Father to send him more than twelve legions of angels in his defense, had he preferred to exact punishment from the wicked rather than to forgive the injury of his own slaughter.

He therefore ordered the edge of the drawn blade to be put away in the guarding scabbard, since he had come, of course, to lay down his own life for all, not to take anyone else's. For to Peter himself, when he promised in a confident voice that he was willing even to die with the Lord, he said: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the cock will not crow today until you have denied me three times.” He was not accusing him of unbelief, but revealing the fear of the panic to come.

Soon he was led to the house of Caiaphas, who at that time was chief of the priests according to the rite of the Jewish religion. But since he sat in the seat of pestilence and stood in the way of sinners, he seemed rather to hold the chiefdom of crimes. For the council had begun to be violently inflamed and roused by false witnesses. A thousand lies flew against the Lord, dead in the empty embers of the accusers and not alive with the warmth of good faith, and they all soon perished, spent by the motion of their own lightness, like a raging fire running through dry stubble: the weak fuel does not give it strength to burn the high treetops, and at once collapsing into ash, the flame loses its empty victory.

When no path opened up for their tricks, fraud gave way to force and turned into fury, and the impatient mob armed itself to raise its hands against the Lord. Alas, held back by such dews of tears, wounded by such groans of spirit, I shudder to recall the sacrilegious hands raised against the Lord in the madness of a frenzied riot! The accursed mob did not stop at striking his head with their fists, spattering his face with spit, and beating him with the blows of their palms. Yet he bore everything patiently and gave himself up for our salvation, and for us he committed his holy body to torments. For through those blows of the fist we have the safety of our head; that spittle is the washing of our faces; by these slaps we have obtained everlasting freedom.

But the elder, to whom the Author of truth had foretold everything, since what Christ had marked out as coming could not remain undone, followed the Lord's footsteps right into the house of the chief priest. Three times he was recognized as being one of his disciples, and three times he denied it. And the cock, the herald of day, crowed. When the oracle of the divine decree had been fulfilled, Peter's former senses returned to him as well. Gathering up the memory of his fault, he rebuked himself for the error of forgetting, and with groaning following at once, his sins fled, his offenses departed, and the showers of tears he poured out won sweet pardon through most bitter weeping. Taught, then, by the example of the apostle, we ought to recognize the power and the merit of repentance, so that, relying on such remedies, we may deserve to shut out deadly diseases from the weariness of our souls. If we have been wounded by the harmful poisons of our thoughts or our actions, or even by the contagion of shameful words, let us at once make haste to take refuge in the most healing medicine of repentance, so that, grieving over our fault, we may not grieve under punishment, and weeping over our wound, we may not weep over our death. Yet we must not prepare repentance in advance for errors yet to come, but apply it to wrongs already committed. For those who sin in reliance on indulgence obtain the desired pardon only with difficulty, though many promise it to themselves with presumptuous confidence so that they may sin. Even David, the wonderful prophet, when he asked indulgence for a past error, indicated in this prayer that he had sinned through ignorance, so that he might obtain it more easily: “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorance, O Lord.” What then? Should whatever outrages our youth has committed be kept to be forgiven in old age? Far be it that vices should remain in us and grow old with us! Though divine mercy, in its most gentle and patient long-suffering, has suspended the punishment of judgment, let no hope of impunity drawn from this respite dull us. Rather, like slaves who have long been runaways, let us at least return late to our Lord, asking him, even as old men, for pardon for our slippery youth. Yet it is fitting for every sinner to cut out the ulcer at once with the knives of repentance, while the fault is still fresh, so that the first beginnings of the creeping disease, like the roots of a bitter plant sunk deeper through the neglect of a careless farmer, may not become impossible to tear out completely by any labor. Finally, the same prophet, so as not to seem negligent in making his plea so late for the sins of his youth, added ignorance, so that he might more easily deserve to have his error forgiven by the merciful judge.

So the apostle Peter, too, did not set out to deny Christ, but fell simply and unknowingly into a lapse of forgetfulness. For he who had promised with full devotion that he was willing to die with the Lord could not bear, whatever the danger, to be seen as a stranger to his company. Among other things he had given a magnificent example of his faith, showing that not even the fear of death could separate him from Christ: some time before, hurrying toward him across the middle of the sea, he had thrown himself into the rushing waves, undeterred by any dread of death close at hand.

Meanwhile the day dawned, sadder than the shadows of night, destined to see a new [?] crime; and, with the gloom of darkness removed, it laid open to the people the unspeakable plans of the Hebrew assembly. Then Judas, the latest dragon and a murderer like the earlier poisoner (for as that one, by cutting Adam off from life, so this one, by handing Christ over to death, became the persecutor of the human race), when he saw the Lord being led to Pilate's praetorium and bound in chains, he who looses the chains of sins, the wretch froze and shuddered. He gave the money, the funeral fee for innocent blood, back to its cruel paymasters, and by returning it he emptied himself of the price of the crime, but not of the crime. For what security can the dread of death bring when it is conceived at a point where fear no longer leads to any cure, as the psalm declares: “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear”? That is, at the judgment itself, where fruitless dread has no time or room for correction. Or what confession can help someone already placed in the jaws of hell, since we read: “But in hell who will confess to you?” For Judas, a public parricide who did not fear to dare it, and who slaughtered not merely his own parent but the Author of the whole world, sought the remedy of repentance in vain. After the audacity of his betrayal, the punishment of the sentence already held him, so that the axe laid to the roots of the tree that had borne accursed fruit might cut down completely the useless shoot of the evil trunk and consign it to the cruel fires. He was suddenly seized by a demented fury and contrived a deadly end for himself, although he was in fact saner at that moment, when he avenged upon himself the outrage of the unspeakable conspiracy. Knotting his throat, he tightened the passage of that accursed gullet through which had come the merciless voice that sold the Redeemer of all, and in a noose hung from a beam he expelled his unhappy soul. Small indeed would seem the punishment for so great an outrage, to which no magnitude of torment could be equal. Yet the very kind of his dreadful end, the death of a corpse hanging on high, denies him sight of heaven and forbids him to touch the earth, so that the man guilty of an unheard-of crime, deserving to be expelled by both elements at once, might neither enjoy the air for life nor, laid out in the common manner of men, breathe forth his soul as a man. This form of death also carries another sign of his own downfall: the fact that the faithless deserter met his death high up revealed from what a summit he had fallen. Lately a disciple, now a criminal; lately called an apostle, now called an apostate.

When the Lord stood fearless before the governor's tribunal, like a gentle lamb led out to the slaughter, the accusing people could find nothing worthy of death to charge him with, so in their eagerness to allege sedition they cried out that he had called himself king, he who was plainly present as king. No one should be surprised if a people that loves falsehood dragged the truth into a crime and rejected the starry empire and the divine power, since, ungrateful for the Creator's favors, it once worshiped groves and served idols in obedience. It seems to be one and the same madness, an equal insanity, to have preferred Baal to the Lord then and Barabbas to Christ now. And while the merciful one is killed and the impious one saved, their judgment, erring in both respects, has reversed the way of justice: the author of death is appointed to live, the Author of life is appointed to die. From this, then, all of you who have remained faithless until now, believe at last that Christ suffered for the salvation of the world. His back furrowed with whips and assailed with insults, he embraced every punishment, so that not even the thief who deserved to perish by his own merits should suffer destruction.

Alas, how grim is the edge of the sickle that cut down the harvest of Jewish posterity! For those who demanded the Lord's death, and declared that his blood would remain upon themselves and their sons, crying out in frenzy and shouting, “His blood be on us and on our children,” condemned all the fruit [?] of their offspring, until this stain is washed from them spiritually by the water of him whose blood, sprinkled upon them, holds deadly dominion over them. Alas for the wickedness of the crime you committed, Pilate! In one judgment, or rather prejudgment, you committed so many crimes that, had you recognized them with a foreseeing mind and sought healing, you ought not to have washed your hands alone, but to have bathed your whole body continually in the holy bath of spiritual water. You unjustly flog the just one; as a governor you put a king on trial; a mortal man, you do not tremble to set yourself above God. So you are already held in the chains of the punishment you must pay, because through many wounds you nail the Lord of creation to the cross, and you fear offending Caesar more than you fear Caesar's maker.

When Christ had been handed over to the soldiers for execution and lay under sentence of death, the mysteries of a great sacrament were nonetheless being enacted in the very attire he received when they mocked him in the guise of a king. That he was clothed in a scarlet cloak displayed the bloody look of the death to come. A crown of thorns encircled his head, because he alone, in loving humility, bore the thorns of all the sins that had overrun the human race on every side. He held a reed placed in his hand, truly very like the sceptre of a worldly kingdom, which, because it changes hands so very often, is seen to be fragile, hollow, light and perishable.

Soon he was stripped of the clothes that were not his own and at once dressed in his own, as one about to lay down in death the garment of the body, which he knew he would take back a little later. He would then assume nothing subject to change, since after death he would return and rise again in the full majesty of his flesh.

Nor is this without a share in the divine: that he touched with his lips the wine mixed with bitter gall that was given him, and rejected it from his mouth. It was indeed a wonderful sign that the Lord tasted bitter death and at once scorned its horrible poison by turning his face away.

So, fastened to the high wood of the gibbet, he transformed by his loving devotion the wrath of that accursed ordeal. Cruelty was cast aside and peace ascended the cross. Shedding the light of his limbs on the violent instruments of the cruel timber, he clothed the punishment with honour and dedicated the torment to salvation; and, lovingly sanctifying in himself the very tortures, he made the sign set up for condemnation a thing consecrated by blessedness. And so that no one's mind may wander in ignorance, everyone ought to reason wisely that the shape of the cross gives cause for veneration, the cross which, worthy of adoration, earned the right to bear the Lord, and that it stretches out through the four regions of the world. For when Christ was exposed on the cross with his limbs outstretched, the axis of the East received his head, the western boundary smiled upon his feet, the North shone with his right hand, the South gleamed with his left. And the whole substance of the world, made fruitful by the Creator's body, showed in itself the line of the cross fulfilled along its straight and transverse boundaries, a line it is seen to have borne from the very origin of the first light.

When the soldiers divided his garments among themselves, they cast lots for the tunic to see who should have it, since it was not sewn but woven in one piece from the top throughout, and they thought it wicked to spoil so marvellous a thing. Let the teachers of schism read this and learn what impiety they commit in tearing apart catholic concord. For if sacrilegious and murderous soldiers found it hard to rend Christ's garment, what a crime do they commit who disturb the peace of the Church and never cease to divide the Lord Christ himself by schisms!

The title, too, written to be read in three languages, in Hebrew, Greek and Latin letters, "This is the King of the Jews," could be read placed above the Lord. It does not seem absurd to ask what the meaning of this sacrament is as well, for nothing that is shown to have been done in Christ lacks a great mystery. Why, then, could this title be read written in three languages, when the great Acts of the Apostles bears witness that many and various nations of peoples were by no means absent from Jerusalem? Either a single language could have served these different peoples through an interpreter, or, if Pilate wished to set this before the eyes of all, he would have made it known to the crowd by furnishing it in a greater exchange of languages. But since it was not brought about by human design, let us understand it as fulfilled spiritually. For the true faith and the catholic confession, which was signified in Christ, taught that the one king of the peoples was set forth in a threefold speech. And that the inscription specifically proclaims him King of the Jews, who rules over the whole creation, fits both a worldly cause and a divine purpose. First, because Pilate, whether from fear of Caesar or because of the guilt of his own credulity, defined of whom he called him king, lest, by setting down the bare title of king, he should seem to declare him king in general and to proclaim him against Caesar, and to have become sacrilegious, as it were, by decreeing death against his own ruler as well. Second, because Christ is reverently named King of the Jews, and the whole Gentile world, given over to the worship of idols, when it has been found worthy to receive the sacraments of Christian teaching, will begin to call upon the Son of God from among the sons of Abraham, to whom, as we read, he promised that he would make him, as indeed he did, the father of all nations. Jesus, then, was called King of the Jews, not only of those then present but also of those to come: for they will leave behind the useless roughness of their natural stock, and soon, grafted into the olive of fruitful sweetness by the ointment of holy chrism, they will lose the bitterness of the barren wild olive.

What is more, the savage and harmful mob, its spirit sated by no punishment, set bloodstained men on either side of the Lord, nailed there under the same condemnation, so that the insult of such company might heap further injury on the wounds already inflicted, although the likeness of the sentence did not reflect any likeness of desert. For with the Just One hanging between robbers, the penalty of the three executed men seems equal, but the cause of two of them is different. They are guilty before the world for their crimes; before him the world itself is guilty, the world that was freed from sin by his blood. Yet the Lord, set upon that gibbet, did not lose the rights of his power. From the lofty balance of the cross, as from a royal throne, he looked upon both as an impartial judge and weighed the merits of each in the scale of his divine heart. He chose the one and left the other, not examining the past deeds for which they were paying, but attending to the present difference in their minds. For the one, from whom the savagery of his fierce way of life did not depart even in the peril of death, tore at the Lord with cruel insults and accursed, biting words, like a shaggy goat whose venomous tooth is the enemy of the branch of the sweetest vine, and he spoke in mockery: "If you are the Christ, save yourself and us." But the other, more restrained and of better hope, who in sparing his tongue spared himself punishment, addressed the Lord with suppliant words, bending his eyes, the only free members he had, toward the ground, since the stretched bonds of his wounds kept his hands, which could not be lowered, from the gesture of humility. For after he had rebuked with just reproach his companion, who had already deserved to be parted from him, and had acknowledged the guilt of his own insolence, he prayed to the Lord thus: "Remember me when you come into your kingdom." At once the loving Lord, like a shepherd joyfully gathering up a sheep that has strayed through pathless wilds, spoke to him, saying: "Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise." O wonderful and divine promise! He who was hastening to go down to the underworld says that he is entering paradise, so as to teach more plainly that there is no time at which God is not present everywhere. For in order to rid the mind of the now blessed robber of the fear of death, he did not say only "Today you will be with me," lest he be thought to be announcing burial, but added "in paradise," where a charming loveliness smiles across the fields with unfading flowers, and delight, nourished by watering springs and spread softly and beautifully through the gardens, gladdens everything with welcome sweetness; and there, among leafy branches that no longer deceive with the snare of fruit, that hellish serpent groans that the ancient tiller of the garden now dwells there without falling. So both men, moving in different ways, set out as robbers on paths that diverged, and, bearing down on places far apart, committed by their deeds a violence of different kinds. The one entered the gates of hell, the other burst into the gates above; the one, sunk in deep darkness, passed through the bars of Gehenna, the other, crossing the threshold of bright light, plundered the kingdom of heaven.

Meanwhile the whole world was suddenly darkened, overwhelmed by the shadows of a sudden blindness, and, drenched in a gloomy mass of clouds, it celebrated the funeral rites of the day. The sun withdrew and hid its rays, lay concealed, veiled in a black mantle, and stained the world with the mourning of a strange night. Such was the face the elements deserved to wear when bereft of the comfort of their Father, that they who had rejoiced at his rising should grieve at his setting. For as light shone forth when the Lord was born, so it departed when he died. Then a star shone by day; now one did not appear even at night. But although the light fled and left heaven and earth, it did not remain long in this withdrawal; that it was suspended for just that span of time seemed to accord with a great mystery. For as the face of the world lay overwhelmed by darkness for three hours, so the burial of the tomb enclosed the Lord for three days.

Nor did the earth stand firm then without harm. It trembled in all its foundations as it perceived such things being done, and nature, thinking the end of the world had now come, hung on an uncertain brink, fearing that the highest summit, descending into the underworld, would at once drag the whole mass down with it into death, and that the world would follow its own Author and pour headlong into chaos. But that boundless loving-kindness of the Godhead was hastening in mercy to Tartarus to restore what was lost, not to destroy what had been established.

And when those who had fastened the Lord to the wood of the cross saw such perils occurring, they were by no means dismayed by so many signs, so many unheard-of portents of present terror. On the contrary, when he was thirsty and asked for a drink, one of that most wicked crowd tied a sponge to a reed and held out vinegar to his mouth. O how well that liquid suited the most wicked mind of the Jews, who, having followed worse and the lowest things, were called bastards for the guilt of their unbelief! For just as sweet wines, once they have turned into sour vinegar, are rejected from the cups of every table and thrown away, so this savage and impious nation, which in ancient times had pleased God, is now hateful and utterly to be abhorred.

When, therefore, the Lord had fulfilled all things of his blessed passion, he at once willingly laid down his soul from his holy body by his own act, intending to take it up again voluntarily by his own act, as he did; for he had indeed died, but he was living, his limbs perishing while he did not die in his divinity. Let us hear what John the evangelist reports in his person; for the Lord says to his disciples: "For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, and I will take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again. This command I received from the Father." Who, then, could doubt, or would dare to doubt, that he who was free to lay down his soul when he wished could also take it up again when he pleased, and could work in himself all the more that power which he deigned to display in so many others? Behold, the gates of Tartarus are unbarred, thrown down at Christ's coming; the path back out of hell lies open; rocks are split, the earth is cleft, tombs are emptied of their bodies, a throng of saints comes back to life; and lest faith fail in the believer, the multitude of those rising is recognized.

Then that wonderful temple too, full of ancient religion, seeing that the summit of the greater Temple had fallen, like a sorrowing and groaning foster-child bewailing its own founder, at once tore its veil and showed its bare breast to all, signifying plainly that its inner secrets were to be opened to the Gentiles and to the peoples who would faithfully come, since the Law, which long remained covered under the veil of Moses, has shone forth now that Christ has come to us. Come, tell us, sad and impious Death, where now is that deadly victory of yours, where now the sting that served you on the way to the tombs, you who from the ruin of the first generation, never sated by any funerals, have invaded the human race and been wont to rule wretched frailty with punishing dominion?
